As cities act to shred housing’s red-tape, Boston homes in on parking

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Boston is an expensive place to build housing, and it is one of the priciest places in the country to live.
  • Cutting parking is one path cities are taking to lower construction costs.
  • Recent findings suggest that boulder, Colorado, set a 90-day deadline for deciding affordable housing applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Boston is an expensive place to build housing, and it is one of the priciest places in the country to live. Its City Council has taken a step toward scrapping one costly requirement: parking.

Cutting parking is one path cities are taking to lower construction costs. Others are chasing review time, density and tax incentives, and the changes are landing at the city and county level.

Recent findings suggest that boulder, Colorado, set a 90-day deadline for deciding affordable housing applications. Allentown, Pennsylvania, tied a tax break to affordable units. Lake County, Illinois, outside Chicago, opened all its residential zones to accessory dwelling units.

These local moves come as states test how far they can push cities to build in the name of approving housing affordability. California, Texas and Florida have passed laws that override local zoning authority. Lawmakers there have had to keep tightening them to head off workarounds.

Illinois and North Carolina may be next. Gov. J.B. Pritzker’s housing reform plan, which stalled this year, is expected to return in January.

A shift in political winds in the Tar Heel State may mean lawmakers try once again to pass broad reform after failing multiple times. But they did eliminate off-street parking requirements across most of the state.

More than 120 cities have eliminated parking mandates, according to the Parking Reform Network, an advocacy coalition.

In a recent development, boston could be next. The city’s average asking rent was $3,065 a month in the third quarter, the fifth highest of the 90 markets Cushman & Wakefield tracks, behind San Francisco, New York, San Jose and Long Island. Home construction fell by 14,000 units between 2024-2025 and 2025-2026, according to this year’s Greater Boston Housing Report Card.

In a recent development, the council voted 9-4 on Nov. 18 to remove parking requirements for new residential construction. The zoning commission must now approve the measure before it goes to the mayor.

Abundant Housing Massachusetts, the Commercial Real Estate Development Association, the Greater Boston Real Estate Board and the Environmental League of Massachusetts Action Fund support the measure.

Five years ago, Mayor Michelle Wu signed off on a zoning amendment to remove off-street parking requirements for affordable housing. Wu, who has championed zoning reform, hasn’t said whether she supports the current measure.

“We will evaluate the implications of eliminating parking minimums citywide,” spokesperson Marcela Dwork said in a statement.

Boston’s transportation department states a garage space can cost up to $50,000, but the Pioneer Institute put underground spaces in Boston at $106,000 to $152,000 in late 2025.

It has been revealed that opponents argue the policy leaves out residents who need cars. But real estate professionals in Boston and elsewhere in the country note that such changes don’t mean parking vanishes.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s about letting each Boston project respond to real demand, not one-size-fits-all formulas,” Reginald Jones-Booker, a Berkshire Hathaway agent, wrote on LinkedIn. “Developers can still include parking where it makes sense, but the mandate would no longer force every upcoming home to meet a fixed minimum.”.

Boulder’s council unanimously approved an ordinance on Nov. 19 that sets a 90-day decision deadline for complete applications. It applies to projects in which at least half the homes are affordable to low- and middle-income households.

Site reviews there have taken a median of 277 days over the past two years, according to Boulder Reporting Lab. Staff, not the Planning Board, will decide requests for extra height or reduced open space, and neighbors can appeal.

Industry observers note that the rules take effect Dec. 19. They are meant to keep Boulder eligible for Proposition 123, a 2022 voter-approved measure that sends state income tax revenue to affordable housing in cities that commit to growing their affordable stock by 3% a year.

Billy Joel’s 1982 hit “Allentown” made the Lehigh Valley city a symbol of a fading industrial America. Bethlehem Steel, the region’s anchor, ended most steelmaking in 1995 and was dissolved in 2003.

Those days are long gone, but the city now faces a different problem: keeping housing within reach as the region grows.

In a recent development, the City Council voted unanimously Nov. 18 to pass a workforce housing ordinance. Developers of projects with 10 or more units who receive a tax break under the Local Economic Revitalization Tax Assistance Act, a 1977 Pennsylvania law known as LERTA, must make at least 20% of the units affordable. Those units are rent-restricted for households earning 60% to 120% of area median income.

The city has no LERTA zone yet, so a council member stated the amended version “does not directly impact workforce housing today.”.

It has been revealed that lake County amended its Unified Development Ordinance on Nov. 10, effective that day, to allow accessory dwelling units in all county residential zones. It also lowers their minimum lot sizes, adds incentives for conservation developments and creates an “early assistance” process for developers. The rules reach only unincorporated areas.

The county acted while the state stalled. Gov. J.B. Pritzker’s Building Up Illinois Developments blueprint, known as BUILD, would have legalized accessory dwelling units statewide, allowed missing-middle housing, set permit-review deadlines, ended excessive parking minimums and standardized impact fees.

In a recent development, it failed to advance before the spring session ended, after the Illinois Municipal League and suburban mayors objected to its zoning mandates. Pritzker has stated the proposal will likely wait until January.

After Pritzker’s plan stalled, Illinois REALTORS revived its Illinois Housing Supply Accelerator Program, launched in August. The program asks local officials to form working groups targeting barriers to building.

Sources indicate that pritzker mentioned in October that he expected BUILD to wait until the full session starting in January. Lawmakers finished the first week of the fall veto session without major housing action. They return Dec. 1-3.

According to recent reports, the reset is not a routine wipe, so XRPL’s Testnet depended on a single full-history server that crashed and could not be recovered. Ripple states it is increasing storage capacity to address the problem and reduce how frequently the network needs resetting.

In a recent development, developers will lose their existing setups and need to collect fresh test XRP from the faucet. Those running their own servers will also need to clear their databases and restart them after the reset.

Recent findings suggest that testnet is used to mirror Mainnet’s amendment status, while Devnet gives developers a place to experiment with proposed features. Both serve as sandboxes, meaning the reset won’t touch real XRP or live ledger activity.

A clean testing environment matters when teams are building latest applications, experimenting with features, or checking integrations before they reach the live network. Losing existing test data is inconvenient, but keeping a broken full-history server running isn’t much of an option either.

So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.
  • Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn.
  • Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The firm expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft claims the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

It has been revealed that the offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

Industry observers note that all of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in upcoming hires.

It has been revealed that the worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a tech giant right now?

Recent findings suggest that harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one firm.

In a recent development, hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more notable than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

Sources indicate that the jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

In a recent development, AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software firm.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a tech giant.

According to recent reports, software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

According to recent reports, this cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

In a recent development, the true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue swiftly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

In a recent development, one venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

1) Think VERY significant, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a tech giant that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

According to recent reports, 3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

Sources indicate that there are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

In a recent development, whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Substantial Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a organization of their own or a year with their family.

Benzinga News, Company Logos and Market Data Now Available Through Alpheya's AI-Powered Wealth Platform for Financial Institutions.

Sources indicate that DETROIT, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Benzinga, a leading provider of real-time financial news and market intelligence, today confirmed an expanded data relationship with Alpheya, a wealth technology manufacturer headquartered in Abu Dhabi. Through this relationship, Alpheya will make Benzinga's real-time news and broader suite of data products available to banks and wealth management institutions.

Alpheya works with banks, family offices, and asset and wealth managers. Its platform gives these institutions a single cloud-based, AI-powered system for client apps, portfolio management and trading.

Many banks and private banks are now modernizing the digital experience they offer clients. To meet that shift, institutions want Benzinga market content inside their own mobile apps, so clients can follow their holdings without leaving the bank's platform. The agreement gives Alpheya's clients a direct path to that content.

Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.
  • Sources indicate that the Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to Upcoming Yorkers’ doors.
  • Recent findings suggest that the legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.

Amazon and Fresh York City are fighting again.

Sources indicate that the Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to Upcoming Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

Recent findings suggest that the legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Sources indicate that companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

In a recent development, on Thursday, Amazon began showing Latest York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

It has been revealed that in a blog post, Amazon stated it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the firm wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”.

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel mentioned the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 Latest Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel stated. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The organization also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

It has been revealed that the standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the manufacturer abruptly canceled looks to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time indicated most Fresh Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6.

Recent findings suggest that city leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”.

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise Upcoming Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”.

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

According to recent reports, amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The manufacturer remarked it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in Upcoming York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty.
  • Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.
  • Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that the OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

Industry observers note that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any firm planning to glitch under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management.".

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:.

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

It has been revealed that for existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

It has been revealed that the Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:.

In a recent development, on diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Recent findings suggest that under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Sources indicate that concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:.

It has been revealed that the difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

It has been revealed that the Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:.

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

Sources indicate that for an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

Recent findings suggest that for now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:.

Industry observers note that both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

Marlowe raises $277M to build inference clusters with chips from Nvidia rivals

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence infrastructure startup Marlowe AI Inc.
  • Bessemer, Altimeter, Emergence Capital and a number of other institutional bakers chipped in as well.
  • Marlowe was founded last year by CEO Dan Lewis and Chief Technology Officer Kutta Srinivasan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:49 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Artificial intelligence infrastructure startup Marlowe AI Inc. has closed a huge $227 million seed round led by Accel.

Bessemer, Altimeter, Emergence Capital and a number of other institutional bakers chipped in as well. They were joined by a large group of angel investors that included the chief executives of Palo Alto Networks Inc, Uber Technologies Inc., Box Inc. and Dropbox Inc. GeekWire reported on Monday that Marlowe is valued at $1.15 billion.

Marlowe was founded last year by CEO Dan Lewis and Chief Technology Officer Kutta Srinivasan. Lewis previously headed the Microsoft Corp. unit responsible for Copilot Studio, the tech giant’s AI agent development tool. Srinivasan was the techical lead of the tech giant’s AI infrastructure group.

Marlowe is building AI data centers for inference workloads. The tech giant will optimize each facility for a specific inference workload category by tailoring its chip mix, network configuration and software. Marlowe believes that its approach will provide better hardware efficiency than general-purpose graphics card clusters.

“Even modest gains in network architecture, power oversubscription, AI-driven fleet operations, and workload-specific inference optimization multiply to create a durable, 2-3x overall advantage in performance, availability, resiliency, and cost,” Lewis and Srinivasan wrote in Marlowe’s launch blog post.

Sources indicate that the firm plans to bring its first data center online  next month. It’s based on hardware from Etched Inc., an inference chip startup that was valued at $21 billion in August.

Graphics cards often use only a small fraction of their maximum clock speed to avoid overheating. Etched’s chip is less prone to overheating and can therefore operate at higher clock speeds, which boosts model performance. The manufacturer says that its accelerator provides “multiple times the FLOPs density” of graphics cards.

In a recent development, etched ships its chips as part of custom-made inference racks. According to the company, the systems feature an interconnect that can perform some data movement tasks more than four times faster than competing silicon. Etched’s rack design also includes custom power management and cooling components.

Marlowe’s second facility will come online in the second quarter of 2027. It will host racks based on Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s Helios design. A Helios rack hosts 72 AMD graphics cards along with central processing units and Pensando data processing units, or DPUs. The DPUs offload networking tasks from the other chips to leave more computing capacity for AI models.

Sources indicate that helios racks’ networking and power delivery links are arranged in a configuration that reduces the need for manual cable maintenance. Additionally, the coolant lines feature a so-called quick-disconnect design. They can be plugged and unplugged without the specialized tools usually needed for the task.

GeekWire reported that Marlowe has also signed a letter of intent for a third data center. According to the publication, each of the company’s planned facilities will provide tens of megawatts of computing capacity. One megawatt is enough to power several hundred homes.

Marlowe will use the proceeds from its seed round to finance hardware purchases and hire engineers.

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has unveiled a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals unveiled a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

It has been revealed that the newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, stated today in a news release.

It has been revealed that “By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith stated. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”.

Sources indicate that mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas remarked.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the price of XRP has continued to slump to deeper levels amid the prolonged market volatility. However, recent onchain data has shown an unexpected trend in exchange activity.

According to the latest data from crypto analytics platform Cryptoquant, XRP is presently facing a severe supply shortage on the world’s largest crypto exchange, Binance.

According to the data, XRP’s Supply Shortage Index on Binance has surged to 2.4 as of November 19 despite the asset’s extreme price weakness in recent days.

Notably, the data further demonstrates that the metric has surpassed the previous reading of 2.09 recorded on July 6, marking a five-month high in XRP’s supply shortage index.

It is important to note that readings above +2 are a strong indication of severely tightened supply, which means that the amount of XRP available on the exchange has decreased significantly.

While negative readings often mean the opposite, this means that XRP has witnessed a sharp reversal from the supply level seen on September 27.

Sources indicate that at the time, the index stood at -1.5 while XRP traded above $1.50, signaling an abundance of XRP on Binance. This means that more tokens were available for trading during the period, which potentially added to selling pressure.

While that is no longer the case, the latest data highlights that the XRP supply index has jumped by 3.9 points in just 53 days, moving from supply abundance to severe supply tightness in just about two months.

This typically suggests that XRP is being aggressively moved out of exchanges despite its prolonged price weakness, potentially driving a rebound in the demand for XRP, which could eventually trigger a price recovery.

Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A customer buys a token on a U.S.
  • In a recent development, under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Sources indicate that open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

It has been revealed that A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app reveals the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

In a recent development, under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Sources indicate that open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

Industry observers note that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

Recent findings suggest that the Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

In a recent development, the CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

It has been revealed that under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks demonstrates where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

In a recent development, the letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

Sources indicate that the CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

GTA VI has a long way to travel to catch its predecessor, though. Take-Two states GTA V has sold nearly 235 million units.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am.

Orchard Robotics, an agtech manufacturer using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was declared Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

Sources indicate that the startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, remarked in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

“Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu stated in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”.

The startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

In a recent development, orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round announced in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

The Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

Bitcoin (BTC), the world’s largest cryptocurrency, is flashing a major, ‘scary’ technical signal that was absent even during its last major crashes in February and June 2026.

The flagship coin has crashed to a fresh 4.5-month low amid persistent institutional outflows totaling billions from cryptocurrency exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

Sources indicate that $BTC hasn't formed a higher high for 16 consecutive days now. This didn't even happen during the Feb 2026 and June 2026 crashes. https://t.co/I6IPmdueEc.

Bitcoin has failed to form a higher high for the past 16 days. This is a very long stretch, one that was absent during Bitcoin’s February and June crashes.

A higher high, in the context of technical analysis, is formed when an asset’s price reaches a new high point above its previous swing high. The absence of higher highs signals that buyers are having a hard time taking back control of the market.

The latest Bitcoin price action adds further to concerns surrounding the future of the flagship cryptocurrency.

Earlier today, BTC crashed to $61,225, its lowest price point in around four and a half months.

Bitcoin's failure to create higher highs despite several attempts to recover shows that selling pressure remains quite high.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, this technical pattern of 16 days without a higher high does not necessarily spell more pain for Bitcoin. If the cryptocurrency can decisively push above recent resistance zones, it may be a sign that buyers are starting to make a comeback.

Bitcoin is facing persistent withdrawals of huge amounts of money from U.S.-based spot Bitcoin ETFs.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) witnessed its biggest-ever daily net outflow on Nov. 19.

Sources indicate that the crypto fund suffered a whopping $541.1 million in net withdrawals on the day. At the same time, total net outflows from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs amounted to around $582.3 million across the entire market.

More alarmingly, the fresh wave of withdrawals brings cumulative net outflows from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs to around $3.47 billion so far this November.

The ETFs have seen negative net flows on 12 of the first 14 trading days of the month.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Silicon Valley divorce lawyers are seeing surge in outreach from CEOs, founders, and high-net-worth employees who are citing the Nvidia scandal as the reason for their calls.

The revelation of Jensen Huang’s affairs, and Nvidia’s board subsequently firing him from the tech giant he founded, is a “precautionary tale for other CEOs,” remarked one lawyer who has been involved in the high-profile divorces of some of the tech industry’s most famous CEOs.

Although Huang’s board reinstated him on Monday in a controversial move, the roller coaster of events has pushed other CEOs to think about how their assets are connected, and potentially at risk, as a result of their personal relationships. In addition to pursuing prenuptial agreements, many are interested in drafting nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) for their significant others, which is a latest trend, claims Monica Mazzei, a partner in Buchalter’s San Francisco family law office.

“It’s totally changed the landscape,” stated Mazzei. “I’ve never seen this before. This was definitely major news in the family law space.”.

According to recent reports, since the Nvidia scandal broke, three clients have contacted Mazzei with requests to draft NDAs for the significant others of CEOs. They specifically cited Huang in the outreach, mentioned Mazzei, who specializes in representing high-net-worth clients. Most of the requests are coming from the firm, not the CEO themselves, in an effort to protect the business.

“The tech giant is probably telling the CEO, ‘Anyone you need to date needs to sign this because we don’t want you to end up in a Jensen Huang situation,’” Mazzei remarked.

Sources indicate that huang had at least three known affairs, two with internal Nvidia employees, and one extra controversial relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at the Singapore-based organization Megaspeed. Alice Huang is reportedly suspected by some intelligence officials of being a Chinese spy and of illegally providing Chinese companies access to advanced Nvidia chips. The allegations are that Alice Huang is a “honeypot” who lured Jensen Huang into a relationship to get access to proprietary information.

“Why honeypots work is because when you’re dating someone you’re not thinking about what they might overhear on a phone call, or see on papers lying out at home,” mentioned Mazzei. “They’re just in your life, overhearing a lot.”.

Demand for prenuptial agreements has also surged. Jensen and Lori Huang have been married for 41 years, and reportedly do not have a prenuptial agreement. Jensen Huang is one of the richest people in the world, with a net worth of roughly $137 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. According to California law, Lori stands to come away with half of that in a potential divorce, along with shares in Nvidia.

It remains to be seen if Lori Huang will file for a divorce. If the couple were to decide to split up, Lori and Jensen Huang would most likely agree to a settlement prior to the divorce proceedings becoming public, says Mazzei. Once the terms are finalized, Mazzei reckons, the couple would then go public with the news, as Jeff Bezos and Mackenzie Scott did.

Libby Leffler, founder and CEO of thisfirst.com, an online prenup service, states she’s seen more customers naming tech billionaires and founders as the inspiration for their agreements since the Nvidia scandal broke. Most of Leffler’s clients are founders and early employees at pre-IPO companies, especially in California and Upcoming York. Every time a public figure’s divorce or prenup makes headlines, Leffler’s inbound requests jump, but the naming of tech CEOs this time is different.

“People used to name-check celebs, but now they are name-checking tech CEOs,” Leffler tells Fortune. “What they really mean is that they want to feel as protected as they assume those people are.” The most referenced arrangement is Jeff Bezos’s rumored prenuptial agreement with Lauren Sánchez, who became his second wife in 2025.

“Your relationship and your cap table are more connected than people think, and founders are seeing that play out,” Leffler mentioned.

According to recent reports, mazzei also noted a surge in prenup requests, specifically coming from Anthropic employees. When the firm went public at a $1.5 trillion valuation on Nov. 19—a week after Huang’s ousting—it minted thousands of multimillionaires among the company’s relatively small staff of 5,300. The average fortune of its non-founding staff is roughly $44 million, although nearly 600 pocketed at least $100 million.

Recent findings suggest that mazzei could not link the Anthropic employees’ requests to Nvidia directly, although the Huangs’ lack of a prenup may have spooked them. In general, many of them are on the younger side, and Mazzei noted that among younger generations prenups are becoming more common.

Shiba Inu’s layer-2 network, Shibarium, is experiencing a major slowdown as daily network activity has fallen to three-digit figures (fewer than 1,000 transactions), hitting lows not seen in months.

According to recent reports, shibarium processed 546 transactions, according to Shibariumscan data, marking a slower period for the layer-2 network after activity spiked to a high of 6,370 on October 31, 2026. Transaction activity declined afterward, and the decline intensified amid the sell-off that hit the market in recent weeks.

The latest figures suggest that fewer transactions are taking place across Shibarium compared with periods of stronger activity. The key question now is whether Shibarium can regain momentum in the coming weeks.

Meanwhile, development continues behind the scenes for the Shiba Inu layer-2 network, as long-time Shiba Inu community member and developer Mazrael revealed a substantial batch of contracts deployed on Puppynet, Shibarium's testnet.

But in the meantime, Shibarium’s fall to three-digit activity levels is a major slowdown that SHIB holders and ecosystem watchers will be watching closely.

Shiba Inu's on-chain holders increased as the number of wallets holding SHIB hit 1,700,930 on November 19, 2026.

According to the latest figures shared by Etherscan SHIB, an X account dedicated to providing updates on the SHIB ecosystem, the cryptocurrency added 236 upcoming on-chain holders in a single day, taking its total past the 1.7 million milestone.

It has been revealed that the month of November has also seen consistent growth, with SHIB adding 4,520 holders since the start of the month. The broader 2026 trend is even more pronounced, with the number of holders of the token increasing by 152,300 since the beginning of the year.

While Shiba Inu's latest milestone seems remarkable, Mazrael suggested that the Shib ecosystem, including Shibarium, might have more holders than indicated, with 1.4 million holders of Binance-pegged SHIB on the BNB Chain.

"Shibarium has more holders than those you listed, though. But yeah. Well, there are also 1.4 million holders of Binance-pegged SHIB on BNB. But that's not actually CCIP SHIB; it is a peg," Mazrael wrote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most people who see something odd on Instagram mutter “huh, neat,” and keep scrolling. Michael Ramsey bought a plane ticket to check it out in person. The former oil and gas marketer, who once ran an F45 studio in Port Melbourne, saw a post about an exercise machine called the Rowformer, and flew from Australia to Orange County to try it himself. Seven years later, STRONG Pilates has more than 130 studios across multiple countries and continents, 57,000 members and more than $75 million in net revenue over the past 12 months.

Ramsey shared how the STRONG brand came together, why some Pilates traditionalists hate it, and why he is totally okay with that.

This wasn’t your original career path. How did you get involved in Pilates?I was working in oil and gas, and I was not enjoying my life too much. I wasn’t highly motivated in corporate. And on the weekends, I was actually running a nightclub with my business partner, Mark Armstrong, who I’ve been in business with for eleven years. And he tapped me on the shoulder and he noted, “Hey, I found this really unique boutique concept called F45 Training.” This was about twelve years ago. And so we actually brought the first F45 studio to Melbourne, Australia, and I quit my job in corporate, and for the first time in my life, I felt free, like I was in charge of my own destiny. Not only did I have financial freedom, but I had time as well. We scaled our F45 studios to six very swiftly, sold after about four or five years.

It has been revealed that what inspired STRONG?My housemate showed me an Instagram post about this Rowformer machine that was created out of Orange County. And to me it ticked a lot of boxes — you’ve got rowing, and you’ve got the Reformer. So I jumped on a plane, took the class and it was one of the most exhilarating, endorphin-led kind of workouts I’d ever done. I’m looking around the room, and there are all these incredibly fit women in their forties and fifties that just looked incredible. And I’m like, “Wow, this, this is awesome. I need to take this back to Australia.” Mark tried it, had the same experience, and then we negotiated global rights for the machine and built a franchise model around it.

Most of us see something cool on Instagram and keep scrolling. We don’t jump on a plane. What does that say about you?Look, to be transparent, it was very opportunistic. I could see, and nothing against F45, but I couldn’t see the lifetime value of the customer increasing over time due to the impact of workouts. So I was on the hunt for something that was low impact, more longevity-focused. How do we keep our members for five, six, seven, ten years? That was a question that I had and the problem I was trying to solve.

How do you turn early adopters into paying clients and repeat customers?You need to respect your product and business enough to have people paying from the start. There’s this whole thing in the fitness industry about free trials, and do they work or do they not work? We are a premium product, and I think once the work is done and the product is ready, you need to respect yourself and your product by charging for every session.

It has been revealed that now, for anyone who’s starting in this space, I would say the first thing to do is just start. Just open, and then learn from your consumer and innovate like crazy. And that’s all we did. It’s a very different product today than what it was seven years ago, and in another seven years it’s gonna be probably even more different, because that’s how it works. If you don’t innovate, you will recede, and you will die.

In a recent development, was there an innovation that came from customer feedback and made you think, “Oh yeah, that’s a good idea”?The big one was the TV screens. Our male audience, as soon as we put TVs in, their trial-to-member conversion went through the roof. You’ve got to imagine, seven years ago, a lot of men hadn’t even experienced Pilates before. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:30 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc. released today with $100 million in funding.

In a recent development, the capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp. He established Epochal earlier this year with two other xAI co-founders, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss. The organization’s staff also includes former researchers from Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Google DeepMind.

Sources indicate that epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal. According to the tech giant, it enables developers to train AI models that can predict future events. The service does so by providing models with access to historical web data from the past 30 years.

Sources indicate that if a bank wishes to train an AI that can predict quarterly earnings, it could use the service to fetch financial results from the first three quarters of 2025. It could then ask the AI to estimate fourth quarter results from the same year. After the model generates its predictions, developers can compare them against real fourth quarter earnings to check the model’s accuracy. They can make adjustments if necessary and then repeat the training workflow until the model starts generating accurate forecasts.

Industry observers note that the Epochal Time Portal features more than 1 trillion historical web pages on launch. Each entry includes a timestamp that indicates when it was created. According to the manufacturer, its timestamps make it possible to track how a webpage changed over time.

Sources indicate that AI models access the content through a purpose-built search engine. It enables them to specify the time periods from which they wish to retrieve webpages. According to Epochal, its platform provides one-minute granularity for the most frequently updated pages.

Like consumer search engines, the Epochal Time Portal prioritizes the webpages that are most relevant to each given query. The difference is that it considers webpages’ creation date when evaluating relevance. If a query contains the term “Meta” but asks for pages created before 2021, the year Facebook Inc. rebranded, the Epochal Time Portal will not bring up pages that relate to the social networking giant.

Industry observers note that today’s frontier models can determine that they’re being trained on historical data rather than up-to-date information. For example, a model might compare the creation date of a webpage to the virtual clock of the operating system on which it deployed. Such discrepancies can decrease the effectiveness of training runs.

According to Epochal, its service mitigates the issue by deploying AI models in sandboxes synced to their training data. If a company is training a model on webpages from 2025, the Epochal Time Portal will run it on a Linux version from that year. It applies the same precautions to the software tools and programming language versions that models use.

Recent findings suggest that the Epochal Time Portal is initially available in a single free tier with low usage limits. Epochal aims to follow up the launch by sharing the results of several AI experiments that its researchers have carried out using the service.

StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.
  • StepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft.
  • Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.

StepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a new round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

Industry observers note that stepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The company has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

Recent findings suggest that the problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

According to recent reports, “A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”.

It has been revealed that sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It has been revealed that it gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer stated an investigation was underway.

Sources indicate that that’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has noted the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

In a recent development, it also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor stated up to 5,000 users may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity says it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

Industry observers note that how it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

It has been revealed that more than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the company states, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

It has been revealed that stepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a company’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-newly introduced releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

In a recent development, along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

According to recent reports, stepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

In a recent development, growth spurt: StepSecurity says its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

What’s next: StepSecurity looks to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The organization states it also intends to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

Private equity deals in sports doubled in the past two years: Investors see it as an ‘institutional-grade asset class,’ Apollo’s Torsten Slok claims

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that private equity is coming for America’s favorite pastime, America’s game, and almost every other sport.
  • “Private equity deals in global sports have roughly doubled from about 100 a year in 2021–2023 to almost 200 in both 2024 and 2025, a sign that investors increasingly see sports as an institutional-grade asset class,” Slok wrote in a Nov.
  • The investment boom isn’t just limited to stakes in pro teams, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that private equity is coming for America’s favorite pastime, America’s game, and almost every other sport. Private equity firms are buying into sports at twice the pace they were a few years ago, according to Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok.

“Private equity deals in global sports have roughly doubled from about 100 a year in 2021–2023 to almost 200 in both 2024 and 2025, a sign that investors increasingly see sports as an institutional-grade asset class,” Slok wrote in a Nov. 22 analysis.

The investment boom isn’t just limited to stakes in pro teams, however. Private equity firms also target the businesses that supply, support and monetize sports, from equipment manufacturers to talent agencies to training facilities.

On Nov. 19, Swiss investment firm Partners Group agreed to acquire a majority stake in Rawlings Sporting Goods—the manufacturer of baseballs, gloves, bats, and protective equipment for MLB. The company serves as the league’s official supplier of game balls, gloves, helmets, face guards, and bases. The league itself owned a stake in the company as well, meaning unlike the minority stakes leagues allow in their teams, the deal gives a private equity firm control.

According to Partners Group, MLB and Rawlings’ existing shareholders will retain meaningful ownership while also giving the Swiss firm exposure to Rawlings’ broader business—which includes brands like Easton and Combat, as well as D-BAT Academies, a network of 228 indoor baseball and softball training facilities.

“Rawlings’ iconic brands and training footprint helps reinforce participation in America’s pastime and has credibility with consumers and athletes across all ages,” Partners Group managing director, private equity goods and products, Thomas Clark said in a press release. “We look forward to working with [CEO Ron Ostrowski], the Rawlings team, and MLB as long-term partners.”.

It has been revealed that apollo has its own sports arm as well: In August, Apollo Sports Capital became a “strategic investment partner” to MLB’s most iconic franchise—the New York Yankees. The deal was a $2.6 billion financing agreement with Yankee Global Enterprises, the team’s holding tech giant, supporting the “continued growth” of the Yankees franchise while also refinancing its existing debt.

Sources indicate that “Teams and leagues might embrace capital for any number of reasons: to support operating costs, update aging facilities or develop upcoming venues, invest in new technologies, or grow their global reach,” Deloitte’s 2026 Global Sports Industry Outlook report read. “But outside investment brings greater scrutiny, new challenges, and rising expectations around transparency, governance, and financial rigor.”.

In a recent development, for decades, professional sports restricted private equity firms and other institutional investors from owning stakes in their teams. Instead, franchises were controlled by wealthy individuals, families, or ownership groups—mainly from the leagues’ concern about preserving control over teams and maintaining structure.

Sources indicate that that began changing in 2019, however, when Major League Baseball became the first major U.S. professional sports league to permit private equity investments in franchises. The NBA and Major League Soccer followed in 2020, and the NHL lifted restrictions in 2021. The NFL became the last of the four major American sports leagues to approve private equity ownership, in 2024.

But those permissions came with limits. According to Sportico, MLB allowed institutional investors to own up to 30% of a franchise, with a single fund capped at 15%. The NBA and NHL permit up to 30% institutional ownership per team as well, but cap individual funds at 20%. The NFL has the strictest ownership rules, only allowing approved private equity firms to own a combined stake of up to 10% in a team—and only 10% in an individual fund as well.

It has been revealed that and the owners have taken advantage of that influx of capital. Outside money helps owners pay for stadium construction, arena renovations, player contracts, and the development of surrounding entertainment districts, all without having to foot the full bill themselves.

Recent findings suggest that for example, the Buffalo Bills created an arrangement in 2024 following the NFL’s lifted restrictions to sell 21% of the team’s stake to a group of limited partners—which included a 10% investment from private equity firm Arctos Partners. The transaction came as the Bills were building their latest stadium, when projected costs rose from $1.4 billion to $2.1 billion.

According to recent reports, but the benefit for private equity owners exists as well. Professional sports teams have access to multiple revenue streams, including broadcasting rights, ticket sales, sponsorships, merchandise, licensing, and stadium-related businesses. The five major U.S. professional sports leagues generated approximately $60 billion in combined revenue in 2025, according to Congress. The estimated combined value of their franchises reached approximately $560 billion that year.

Industry observers note that “The upcoming model of baseball—or basketball, football—is teams becoming media companies and transcending a local marketplace,” Rashaun Williams, founder and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners, which held a minority stake in the newly relocated Las Vegas Athletics MLB team, previously told Fortune. “They’re finding ways to diversify their revenue and monetize that fan base 365 days a year.”.
