📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that betsy Fore was raised in rural Illinois, but she often made the 17-hour drive to the Turtle Mountain Reservation in North Dakota, where her mother grew up. To this day, Fore’s uncle owns an auto body shop there; as a child, she helped him, and her father, tinker in the garage.

Recent findings suggest that “It was like, If you can dream it, you can build it,” Fore recalls. “So I believed that. That was really my start as an entrepreneur because I believed I could kind of do anything.”.

Fore has spent the past two decades as an inventor, CEO, serial entrepreneur and investor.

It has been revealed that she rolled out WonderWoof, one of the first dog activity monitors, in 2014. She was the co-founder and CEO of Tiny Organics, a tech giant delivering organic, nutrient-rich meals for babies and toddlers. Her nonprofit career accelerator, Natives Rising, empowers indigenous communities with technology, entrepreneurship and wellness.

It has been revealed that at the moment, she’s the founder and managing director of Velveteen Ventures, investing in solutions for children and the planet for the next seven generations. “Velveteen was built on my deep inner why. Before you build anything externally, you have to excavate why you’re building it at the level of your soul — not just your resume.”.

What’s more, Fore just announced the launch of Velveteen Labs, a first-of-its-kind studio model that allows children to be shareholders in incubated companies. Shares are placed into a trust, and when the children turn 18, they give a majority of them to a cause of their choice.

“She’s showing that investing in Indigenous and Gen Alpha-focused founders isn’t a trade-off between impact and returns,” Roy Swan, director of mission investments at Ford Foundation and author of Positive Sum: How Zero-sum Thinking Broke Capitalism—and How We Can Fix It, indicates. “It’s simply good investing, done with the next seven generations in mind.”.

Sources indicate that needless to say, Fore has accomplished a lot over the course of her career, and she’s met many entrepreneurs along the way. There’s one thing that always gets her very excited within the first five minutes of a conversation: when the person has a unique insight, based on lived experience, into the problem they set out to solve.

“You can just see when someone is speaking from their authentic self,” Fore explains. “It’s not really a sales pitch at that point. They’re literally saying, ‘I’ve tried everything. This is what worked for me. This is how I’m going to try to bring it to market.’”.

Entrepreneur sat down with Fore to learn exactly how founders can reach that authentic place and accomplish the goals they set for themselves.

Fore’s book, Built on Purpose: Discover Your Deep Inner Why and Manifest the Business of Your Dreams, “breaks down how to go from idea to making something real through a values-driven approach,” Michael Acton Smith, co-founder of meditation space organization Calm, shared in a statement.

Uncovering that deep inner why, and bringing the idea to life, starts with lessening the focus on external relationships — with customers, investors, and board and team members — and looking inward, Fore says.

According to recent reports, fore highlights the centuries-old practice of anchoring as an example of how to kick off the process. “ When yogis put their index finger and thumb together in meditation, it’s not just a pose,” she explains. “That gesture is a signal through your nervous system. It’s connecting your individual consciousness to something larger than yourself.”.

Sources indicate that fore encourages founders to build their own version of that practice, and it begins with identifying your values. For instance, in her own life, Fore draws on the seven grandfather teachings that guide her Turtle Mountain Chippewa tribe: love, respect, bravery, truth, honesty, humility and wisdom.

Whatever your individual values are, the next step is to physically anchor and embody those values day to day, Fore notes.

“Lean into them with a gesture, a breath, a word, so that when you walk into a fundraising meeting or have a hard call, you’re not operating from the scarcity mindset, but instead one of abundance,” Fore says. “You’re operating from who you actually are.”.

Manifesting the results you want to see also plays a key role in success, Fore says.

A study conducted by Dr. Gail Matthews, a psychology professor at Dominican University of California, showed that people are 42% more likely to achieve their goals if they write them down every day.

Fore recommends opening your laptop each morning and starting with a simple sentence.

It has been revealed that “Write it in the ‘I am’ present moment,” Fore explains. “I am building this for. I am building this because. So it’s not the pitch. It’s the real reason. The act alone changes your follow-through at a neurological level, if you’re able to live as if it’s already happening.”.

Sources indicate that additionally, Fore says a therapeutic model called Internal Family Systems (IFS), developed by Dr. Richard Schwartz in the 1980s, can support in taking the next step toward a desired future.

The idea is that we’re not one unified self; we’re a whole system of parts, and each one has a job to do, Fore says.

“ Some of them are what IFS calls exiles, and those are the wounded or the younger versions of us that formed in hard moments in our life, the ones that carry the shame or the fear, the grief,” she explains. “Essentially, embodying that sort of scarcity mindset. And then there are the protectors, the parts that showed up to keep those exiles safe. For instance, your inner critic, that’s a protector.”.

According to recent reports, A lot of leadership advice tells people to push past fear, silence their inner critic and be more confident to get what they want. However, while Fore acknowledges there can be some value in that, she also believes that being afraid can only get you so far. Instead of simply fighting fear, she encourages founders to engage with it.

“Literally, out loud or in your head, identify it and ask what that part wants — the answer incorporates parts you love about yourself and want to bring to the forefront,” she says.

Fore points to difficult conversations with a team as an example. Instead of asking why an matter wasn’t flagged sooner, she can admit that part of her feels frustrated, then express gratitude it was caught.

“ This is a leader who’s not being hijacked by these exiles in the middle of a critical moment,” she notes. “The folks who are winning are thinking differently.”.

When founders do look outward and consider their relationship to customers, they might be using a transactional lens — Fore admits she made the same mistake in the beginning.

Instead, Fore suggests flipping the traditional fundraising model on its head and asking, What if the foundation of every product was built with the customer in mind, and every bit of capital was leveraged to return exponential value to them?

In a recent development, “ That shift from extraction to service is the difference between founders who build loyal communities and founders who churn customers,” Fore says. “So if you can ask yourself every single day, Who isn’t being served right now? That question is where your next great idea lives.”.

Fore put that idea into practice when she released Tiny Organics, which scaled to more than $13 million in sales in 24 months.

Fore sent an email to a local parent group in Park Slope, asking if other people were also interested in getting their babies to eat real fruits and vegetables that didn’t come from a pouch. She received hundreds of messages in response and had to cap the project at 100 families within two hours.

Those 100 founding families helped develop Tiny Organics’ first hero product and led to a series of supper clubs introducing kids to their first 100 flavors; those ultimately expanded to Boston, Atlanta and Chicago.

Fore’s customer-first approach that continues to resonate with the companies Velveteen Ventures invests in today.

In a recent development, “We wanted partners who see caring for families as one of the most key economies of our time,” Emily Greenberg, president and co-founder of AI family assistant Joy Parenting Club, says. “Velveteen leads in the care economy, and Betsy gets it in a way few investors do as a previous founder in this category. She knows that when you support parents, you’re investing in the next generation.”.

These days, in the age of AI, the soft skills have become the hard skills, Fore states, noting they’re the foundation of everything she’s seen actually work in business — and she looks forward to leaning on them now and in the years to come.

“ I have so much hope,” Fore claims. “You can probably tell I’m an eternal optimist. I’m going to turn everything into a victory in life. Then, inevitably it happens, where you’re able to figure it out and find a way. I know that’s been true for me, and for so many of the founders that we funded.”.

Recent findings suggest that betsy Fore was raised in rural Illinois, but she often made the 17-hour drive to the Turtle Mountain Reservation in North Dakota, where her mother grew up. To this day, Fore’s uncle owns an auto body shop there; as a child, she helped him, and her father, tinker in the garage.

It has been revealed that “It was like, If you can dream it, you can build it,” Fore recalls. “So I believed that. That was really my start as an entrepreneur because I believed I could kind of do anything.”.

Fore has spent the past two decades as an inventor, CEO, serial entrepreneur and investor.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

Sources indicate that but a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

Industry observers note that the summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration strategy and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It demonstrates how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository notes a yes vote does two things:.

Sources indicate that it also states plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

According to recent reports, A no vote would stop the whole blueprint. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 indicated an expected result of "Will PASS":.

It has been revealed that turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Recent findings suggest that mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

According to recent reports, the tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC demonstrated almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

In a recent development, why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

In a recent development, for now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • Sources indicate that the bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

Sources indicate that the bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the tech giant’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company claims it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software enhancement that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

According to recent reports, the bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows upgrade used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

Recent findings suggest that the final report doesn’t say what the July upgrade was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Industry observers note that third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

It has been revealed that how it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report indicates.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate concern.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft notes it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

According to recent reports, it also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft claims its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

Recent findings suggest that the report also confirms what Microsoft remarked the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it indicates. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the manufacturer says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled.
  • It has been revealed that the Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov.
  • On Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled. Its size depends on a stock that has swung more than $30 a share in its first three sessions.

It has been revealed that the Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov. 18, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising a record $81.3 billion and valuing the organization at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The stock opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19, closed its first day at $97.17, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday.

On Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way. Shares closed down 1.4% at $87.64, about 5.6% above the IPO price.

Recent findings suggest that techCrunch estimated Thursday that Anthropic’s charitable commitments could be worth about $156 billion at roughly $95 a share, where the stock traded early in its debut. The figure combines the company’s Public Benefit Fund, employees’ pledged shares, and Anthropic’s match on those pledges.

Recent findings suggest that because all three are paid in stock, the total moves with the share price. At Monday’s close, the same math yields about $144 billion, down $12 billion from Thursday. At the $83 IPO price, it would be roughly $136 billion.

Recent findings suggest that even the lower figures are enormous. By TechCrunch’s count, Americans gave $617 billion to charity in all of 2025, so Monday’s value equals nearly a quarter of a year of U.S. giving.

Industry observers note that the largest piece is the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a wholly owned LLC the firm announced in October. Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows it contributed 846.8 million shares to the fund, 5% of fully diluted shares as of June 30, a stake worth about $74 billion at Monday’s close.

Industry observers note that the fund can grow. Anthropic states its board may add another 2% of the firm for every 50% increase in value above a set baseline; TechCrunch reported that baseline is the $83 IPO price, which would put the next trigger near $124.50 a share. The company remarked it will disclose more about the fund’s governance and valuation milestones in the coming months, and it has not announced a distribution timetable.

The second channel is employees. About half of Anthropic’s staff take part in its equity donation program, and the manufacturer matches pledged shares 3-for-1 for longer-tenured employees and 1-for-1 for newer ones, according to plan documents filed with the S-1. TechCrunch estimated employees have pledged about $23 billion in stock, which would draw roughly $53 billion in matches at $95 a share.

In a recent development, that money is closer to moving, but not yet. Most holders face a lockup of up to 180 days, which could end sooner after first-quarter 2027 results, and many employees cannot sell or gift most of their shares until next spring, the Associated Press reported. Shares parked in donor-advised funds, which have no annual payout requirement, may take even longer to reach working charities.

The third channel is the least certain. Anthropic’s seven cofounders have pledged to give away 80% of their personal equity, a commitment the AP valued at $112 billion at the IPO price. But the S-1 describes the pledges as “voluntary, revocable expressions” of intent that are not legally binding, and timing, amounts, and recipients remain undecided. TechCrunch’s $156 billion estimate excludes them.

In a recent development, the cofounders also face the longest lockup: up to 365 days from the Nov. 18 prospectus, or earlier after third-quarter 2027 results, with a portion of their shares eligible for release around the 180-day mark.

Some money is already committed. Earlier this month, Anthropic pledged $50 million to a donor-advised fund at the San Francisco Foundation for Bay Area nonprofits through 2027. The first $500,000 went to the SF-Marin Food Bank, GLIDE, the Interfaith Winter Shelter, and the San Francisco Firefighters Local 798 Toy Program, and a company spokesperson told TechCrunch the gift did not come from the Public Benefit Fund.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic has also committed $200 million to study and address AI’s effects on the labor market. In June, it pledged $150 million to Claude Corps, a fellowship that places early-career workers at nonprofits to help them use AI.

Industry observers note that separately, Anthropic has given $40 million this year to Public First Action, a bipartisan group that advocates for AI safeguards. That is policy spending, not charity, and Anthropic says it will not use equity held by the Public Benefit Fund for lobbying or political giving.

It has been revealed that the next test for the share price comes Dec. 15, when up to 303 million shares can become eligible for sale under the prospectus’s lockup schedule, followed by another 303 million on Jan. 5. For charities, the date that matters more is spring 2027, when employee pledges and the manufacturer’s matches can start to move.

Industry observers note that until then, Anthropic’s philanthropic promise is marked to market every trading day. A return to the $115 debut high would lift TechCrunch’s measure to nearly $190 billion; a slide below $83 would take it under $136 billion.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that we once worked with a student whose college application included, among several supplemental essay prompts, a question about a time they’d disagreed with someone. Such prompts became especially prominent in the wake of Hamas’ October 7, 2023 terrorist attacks on Israel, the ensuing Israel-Hamas war, and the campus encampments and protests that swept American universities. Amid growing polarization on college campuses, universities increasingly emphasized the importance of students engaging respectfully with opposing viewpoints, challenging their own assumptions, and learning across difference.

According to recent reports, the student’s father, however, insisted his child had never disagreed with anyone. His child simply wasn’t disagreeable! Surely, every teenager has disagreed with someone. But rather than help his child identify a meaningful disagreement, the father challenged the very premise of the essay. The irony, of course, wasn’t lost on us. Here was a father being disagreeable simply for the sake of being disagreeable, all while insisting his child had never disagreed with anyone.

These are the kinds of interactions that can consume an extraordinary amount of a college admissions counselor’s time. And they illustrate a lesson every entrepreneur should understand. Sometimes, your most expensive clients aren’t the ones who pay the least. They’re the ones who question everything.

Most entrepreneurs know the Pareto principle, commonly called the 80/20 rule. Roughly 80% of results often come from 20% of efforts. But there’s another side to that equation. A relatively small percentage of clients can consume a disproportionately large share of your team’s time and energy. At Ivy Coach, our college admissions consulting firm, we’ve seen this firsthand.

In a recent development, in another case, a family consulted their student’s school counselor about a Personal Statement we’d helped develop. The counselor recommended scrapping it in favor of an essay about what we call a third-rail topic, one so clichéd in college admissions essays that it can significantly undermine an otherwise compelling application.

It has been revealed that when we had the student ask the school counselor to explain the reasoning behind the ill-advised recommendation, the response came back in prose that appeared to have been generated by artificial intelligence. Our AI detection software flagged it as AI-generated, too. Here was a family paying for specialized college admissions expertise, only to ask our team to defend its recommendations against generic advice that apparently hadn’t even been written by a human. It’s madness!

According to recent reports, there’s, of course, nothing wrong with seeking a second opinion. But there’s a difference between asking thoughtful questions and questioning everything simply because someone else has offered a different opinion, especially when that opinion may have come from a chatbot. For Ivy Coach’s college counselors, every hour spent defending sound advice is an hour that can’t be spent helping another student.

Recent findings suggest that ivy Coach has been in the college admissions consulting business for 35 years, and over the past decade, we’ve noticed a troubling trend. We track exclusions from our college admissions statistics: students who choose not to follow our recommendations. Or, more often than not, whose parents choose not to follow them. And while these families remain a small minority of our clients, their numbers have increased over the last 10 years. In other words, more families are paying for our expertise only to disregard it.

I sometimes wonder whether our increasingly polarized political climate has something to do with it. We’ve grown accustomed to questioning expertise, seeking validation for our existing beliefs, asking AI chatbots to tell us precisely what we want to hear and treating disagreements as contests to be won rather than opportunities to learn. Has that mentality spilled over into relationships between clients and professional advisers, including college counselors? Maybe.

In a recent development, our experience alone can’t establish the cause, but we’ve increasingly encountered families more interested in challenging our recommendations than understanding them. And that raises a question every entrepreneur should consider: What happens when clients pay for your judgment but refuse to heed your advice?

In a recent development, ivy Coach has grown considerably over the years, adding former admissions officers from many of America’s most selective universities. But we’ve remained boutique by design. We deliberately limit enrollment because helping students build compelling applications requires extraordinary individual attention. We can’t provide that attention if a handful of families consume a disproportionate share of our counselors’ time.

According to recent reports, that’s why our initial Complimentary Consultation isn’t simply an opportunity for prospective clients to evaluate us. It’s an opportunity for us to evaluate them. Are they seeking expert guidance or validation? Are they willing to hear advice that contradicts what they’ve read online? Do they understand that college admissions is inherently uncertain?

These warning signs often emerge during that initial consultation. One is the word “guarantee.” No ethical college counselor can guarantee admission to Harvard, Stanford or any other highly selective university. Another is a parent who questions just about every recommendation without showing any willingness to consider the answers. We welcome thoughtful disagreement. We don’t welcome endless arguments for their own sake.

And when we spot these warning signs during that first conversation, as we so often do, we’d rather turn away the business than invite months or years of unnecessary headache.

Entrepreneurs are conditioned to chase growth, but revenue isn’t profitability, and growth isn’t always progress. A difficult client can consume so much of your team’s time that the relationship becomes far less profitable than it appears. Worse, that client can diminish the quality of service everyone else receives.

It has been revealed that for businesses built on specialized expertise, protecting your team’s time isn’t just good management. Rather, it’s a critical responsibility to your other clients. The best college admissions counselors don’t tell parents what they want to hear. They tell them what they need to hear. And the best entrepreneurs recognize that not every prospective client is worth accepting. After all, the most expensive client may be the one you should never have taken on in the first place.

This week on the GeekWire Podcast, longtime Microsoft beat reporter Mary Jo Foley, a GeekWire contributing writer, sizes up where the organization stands after one of its most eventful weeks in years.

Microsoft opened its Ignite conference with an apology for the global Outlook outage, then took direct aim at OpenAI and Anthropic on price, even though it invests in both and sells their models. We discuss the lasting damage from the outage, why enterprise customers have few places to go even when they’re fed up, and Microsoft’s pitch to make Copilot the “OS for work,” as Anthropic goes public.

Mary Jo also explains how Microsoft changed the way it rolls out news at its substantial conferences, what got lost along the way, and what that states about the manufacturer after the shakeup of its communications team. Plus, we weigh who from Microsoft could lead Nvidia, and the GeekWire trivia challenge goes back to 1997.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot indicates its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT.
  • Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

In a recent development, at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot indicates its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

It has been revealed that blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham claims those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

In a recent development, if Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

Recent findings suggest that it reveals how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own owners. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now reveals:.

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:.

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:.

Asset | Held with third-party custodians.

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, demonstrated BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:.

In a recent development, not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

Industry observers note that how Binance notes it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:.

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

According to recent reports, what the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

In a recent development, binance states the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest enhancement says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:.

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

In a recent development, what it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

In a recent development, what customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Sources indicate that binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

XRP has spent a week unable to get back above $1. In November 2026, the token hit a two-year low of $0.895, and on Nov. 20, it was trading near $0.96. XRP is down 27.7% in November and about 51% since January, according to CryptoRank data.

Sources indicate that the last time XRP lost more than 28% in a month was February 2025, when the token fell 29.3%. That month, the crypto market was also hit by a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange on Feb. 21.

XRP did not recover right away. From March to June 2025, the token gained about 4.5% in total, according to CryptoRank. In July 2025, XRP jumped 35%, and on July 18, 2025, it set its all-time high of $3.65. On the same day, U.S. President Donald Trump signed the GENIUS Act, the country's first stablecoin law. XRP is now 73% below that record.

Recent findings suggest that in November 2021, XRP lost 10%, and it fell another 17% in December and 25.6% in January 2022. In November 2022, the month of the FTX collapse, the token dropped 11.8%, and it lost 16.9% in December. XRP finished 2022 down about 59% and gained 20.1% in January 2023.

According to CryptoRank, XRP's median return is -10.2% in November and -4.07% in December.

According to recent reports, soSoValue data shows spot XRP ETFs have lost about $26 million to outflows since the start of November. About $19.1 million of that amount left the funds in the week ending Nov. 13.

On Nov. 19, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse said on CNBC that investors had been selling crypto to buy shares in big listings. "People are taking liquidity out of a very liquid market, crypto included — Bitcoin, XRP — and moving it into SpaceX. The exact same thing happened coming into the Anthropic IPO. What we saw after the SpaceX IPO was a rally in the crypto markets. I think you'll see that happen here as well," he said.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • In a recent development, A large manufacturer was preparing to move a major customer segment onto a upcoming service model.
  • Nobody approved it as final, and nobody stated the firm was committed to that version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, A large manufacturer was preparing to move a major customer segment onto a upcoming service model. One part of the model depended on whether a third-party data feed would be available at the level of detail the company expected. The vendor hadn’t confirmed the final specification, so the program treated the feed as provisional.

Nobody approved it as final, and nobody stated the firm was committed to that version. The program team simply needed a working basis for moving forward while the vendor finished its testing.

According to recent reports, at the weekly program review, the current specification was sent forward to the teams that needed it. The cover note called it “provisional” and listed the vendor confirmation as still open.

Sources indicate that at the next review, the vendor still couldn’t confirm the final specification. The program kept the assumption open because there still wasn’t enough evidence to approve or reject it, while the work that depended on the current version continued.

Within two weeks, the provisional input had started shaping work across the program. Marketing had drafted customer communications using the expected level of detail. Finance had built the service cost estimate around the processing volume that specification would create.

Industry observers note that technology had completed part of the interface configuration, and Operations had started shaping support materials around the information employees expected to receive. None of those commitments looked decisive on its own.

One team had already gone further. Technology had built a field-mapping routine that assumed the vendor feed would include several data elements still under review. The routine could be changed later, but doing so would require reopening testing that other work was already using.

That build step mattered because the interface team had also started testing how employees would use the information during a customer interaction. The screen layout, validation checks and exception handling all reflected the current feed structure. None of that work formally approved the assumption, but another part of the service was now being exercised against it.

Industry observers note that when the vendor finally confirmed that the feed would contain less detail than expected, the change hit several places at once. Marketing had to revise messages that no longer matched the service experience. Finance had to reopen the cost estimate because more manual handling would be required.

The organization had reached the consequences of a decision without ever making the decision itself.

Technology had to revisit the interface and repeat part of its testing, and Operations had to rework guidance that assumed employees would see information the feed wouldn’t provide.

Recent findings suggest that leaders expect a provisional item to remain movable until someone formally approves it. That expectation makes sense because the label states the matter is still open, yet the people doing the work still need a basis for moving forward.

One function prepares customer communication, another estimates cost, and another builds against the best information available. Each commitment is locally reasonable, and none of them settles the question.

Together, they change how much surrounding work has to move if the assumption changes.

In a recent development, this is where the “Broken Handoffs” execution leak appears. The program team hands over an input that’s openly provisional, and the receiving teams turn that input into work of their own. The handoff starts a series of separate commitments that no one reviews as one combined choice.

It has been revealed that the sensible response is to make assumptions more visible. So, teams add labels for “confirmed, provisional and unresolved items.” Handoff templates call out dependencies, and open questions receive owners, dates and review points.

According to recent reports, those changes reduce ambiguity. In this program, the data-feed specification was identified as provisional in the review material, and the vendor confirmation remained visible as an open item. The teams still had work to do while the uncertainty remained unresolved.

According to recent reports, technology kept building the parts of the interface it could complete. Other teams continued their work from the latest available specification because waiting for certainty would have stopped parts of the program that could still move.

The more detailed handoff improved the description of the uncertainty without stopping the commitments growing around it.

That second review tested the assumption in more detail.

The vendor still hadn’t completed the work needed to confirm the final feed specification, so leadership asked whether enough evidence existed to approve the current version and concluded that it didn’t.

Industry observers note that keeping the assumption provisional was the right answer because the underlying question still wasn’t ready for a sound decision. The discussion then moved to what could continue safely while the program waited.

In a recent development, technology remarked it could keep building interface components unaffected by the missing detail. Finance could continue refining the cost view with a range, while customer messaging could move as long as the copy avoided specific promises about the data.

All of that was reasonable, and it also meant the organization continued adding commitments around an assumption that no one was yet able to decide.

According to recent reports, by the time the vendor returned with the final specification, the program wasn’t revisiting one choice. It was dealing with the combined effect of choices made in different places, at different times and for different local reasons.

Recent findings suggest that the usual controls work well when a decision exists. Leaders can ask who approved it, what evidence supported it, when it should be reviewed and whether the basis for it has changed.

Industry observers note that this situation leaves no single decision event to reopen. The assumption can stay correctly labeled as provisional, the review can correctly keep it open, and every team can act reasonably inside its own work.

Separate commitments gradually give the assumption the practical weight of a decision even though the organization never created one. By the time someone asks whether the business should still be operating on that assumption, the answer is already embedded in work spread across several teams.

A working assumption becomes dangerous when the organization no longer needs a decision for it to start behaving like one.

Industry observers note that the 1999 FIFA Women’s World Cup final was a watershed moment for women’s football, with record-breaking attendance and viewership numbers. More than 40 million people in North America tuned in to watch the U.S. beat China 5–4 on penalties in the final. Among them was ­ Canadian Nikki Doucet, then a student and college basketball player at St. Francis Xavier University. “That was the first time I’d seen women’s team sports on TV, and I remember feeling so excited,” she states.

In a recent development, since then, interest in women’s football has grown significantly. Its global fan base is projected to surpass 800 million by 2030, according to Nielsen Sports, while Fifpro expects the sport to be a $1 billion industry by 2027—a 72% increase from 2024.

Industry observers note that now CEO of Women’s Super League Football, the manufacturer responsible for operating the top two English women’s leagues (WSL and WSL2), Doucet is at the sharp end of that opportunity. England has become a commercial force in women’s football: Eight of the world’s 15 highest-revenue clubs are in the WSL, according to Deloitte, and Doucet believes the league is well-positioned to capture a “significant portion” of the potential $1 billion the sport is predicted to generate.

American entrepreneurs and investment groups are taking note. The success of the Women’s National Basketball Association—now an $850 million franchise—and the soaring valuations of teams in the National Women’s Soccer League (league leaders Gotham FC were recently valued at $350 million) underlines the potential. And many see an opportunity to buy in at an early stage in the commercial development of the sport in Europe.

U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL promotion. Other notable investors include Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian, who holds a minority stake in Chelsea FC Women, and U.S. financier Marc Zahr, an investor in Aston Villa Women.U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL promotion. Other notable investors include Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian, who holds a minority stake in Chelsea FC Women, and U.S. financier Marc Zahr, an investor in Aston Villa Women.

Speaking at the WSL’s New Playbook ­ summit earlier this year, one investor argued that European women’s football represented the “best opportunity in sport,” on a risk-adjusted basis.

According to recent reports, “I think of my career as if I’m still an athlete. I practice for every board meeting in the same way that I used to train for a game. Your practice should be so hard, the game is easy.”.

Industry observers note that “The enterprise value of these clubs is 100% going up,” Doucet, a former investment banker at Citi, claims. “The question is, do you have owners that want to participate in this asset class of women’s football? There are different tradeoffs versus men’s football and different risk factors because we’re in a different stage of development.”.

It has been revealed that doucet’s challenge is turning rising global interest in the women’s game into regular paying customers. There was a surge in interest following the England Lionesses’ UEFA Women’s Euro 2022 victory: Average attendance at WSL matches tripled to 5,616 the following season. But last year, median attendance was 3,236—and it remains heavily concentrated in a few clubs.

Recent findings suggest that “This isn’t a manufacturing challenge. This is a marketing and revenue challenge,” Doucet notes. The league invested in a rebrand of both the WSL and WSL2 ahead of the newly expanded league this season, and clubs are also investing more. In April, WSL team Brighton confirmed prepares to build Europe’s first purpose- built women’s football stadium at an estimated cost of more than £75 million ($99 million).

“You have to invest in building the foundations that will generate long- term returns, but they might take time until you actually see the results,” Doucet says. “That’s the constant tradeoff.”.

The underlying economics also remain fragile. Despite the high revenues, only four of the 14 clubs in the WSL recorded a profit (two clubs did not publish detailed financial data). The league itself, which is co-owned by the participating clubs, posted an operating loss of £8.2 million ($10.8 million) for the year ending July 2025.

In a recent development, doucet attributes much of the loss to one-off costs associated with becoming an independent business, including establishing its own HR, finance, legal, and regulatory teams. The WSL and WSL2 formally split from the Football Association (FA) in 2024, shortly after Doucet joined the organization. She indicates the league is now profitable, although declined to share the financial details.

“We’re in a transition phase, which is probably a little bit messy. The challenge is going from massive structural moments, like a World Cup, to building a weekly fan habit around women’s professional football,” Doucet notes.

It has been revealed that the majority of the league’s revenues so far have come from broadcast rights and commercial partnerships. The league generated £8.7 million ($11.5 million) from Sky and the BBC in 2025, and the league counts Doucet’s former employer Nike, in addition to Airbnb, Apple, and ­ Barclays, among its growing list of sponsors.

The opportunities for commercial sponsors are different from those in the men’s sport, Doucet indicates. “We have a different audience that really values companies that are investing in women’s football,” she says. “They’re very brand loyal, and they show much deeper engagement.”.

It has been revealed that doucet’s current priority is improving the spectacle on the pitch. “The fans want to watch the best players, and they want to watch a competition that’s exciting and has jeopardy,” she says. Good progress has been made in this area, too. The London City Lionesses signed three-time Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas from Barcelona this summer, and the WSL had the highest representation of players at last year’s Women’s Euro tournament of any league.

Industry observers note that ensuring the WSL’s longevity is a responsibility Doucet is acutely aware of. “This isn’t a five-year business,” she claims. “This is a generational asset.” She remains optimistic about what lies ahead. Doucet adds: “We’re in an early stage, so the potential is almost completely untapped—you don’t know how big it could be.”.

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 glitch of Fortune with the headline “Women’s football has a $1 billion opportunity—and the WSL wants a slice of the pie.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, italy’s largest banking group, Intesa Sanpaolo, increased its spot altcoin ETF holdings according to a new disclosure. This follows capital rotation out of Bitcoin products by a slew of traditional firms amid dwindling market sentiment.

The bank’s disclosed crypto ETF holdings grew in Q3 2026 to $108.56 million, up $17 million, while digital asset prices moved sideways. In June, total assets were worth $90 million as it looked to diversify and grow holdings systematically.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin, the largest asset in the portfolio, was reduced to make room for altcoins in a possible bid to diversify assets. At the end of Q2, BTC holdings stood at $69.32 million but dropped slightly to above $61 million last quarter. The firm’s Ethereum exposure also dropped to $5 million.

However, Solana and XRP products filled the vacuum, highlighting institutional appetite for these assets. At the time of writing, the bank’s spot Solana ETF exposure is at $14.1 million after its investment in the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF ballooned from seven shares to 875,407 shares.

Intesa’s XRP investment also grew over the same period to $27.2 million, driven mainly by 402,750 shares in the Bitwise XRP ETF. The firm’s shares in the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF remained unchanged across both quarters.

Sources indicate that more broadly, the bank reduced its Bitcoin ETF exposure and increased SOL and XRP products. Most experts believe it follows the current market trend, and firms, especially traditional companies, need to diversify to make up for Bitcoin’s decline.

In a recent development, historically, during bear phases, there’s a huge rotation of capital into altcoins, though it’s not sustained for long. As expected, Solana and XRP become institutional favorites, while Ethereum trades similarly to Bitcoin.

The former have the potential to record spikes within the red wave, like in 2022 before the approval of spot ETF products in the United States. These products opened up digital assets to a new stash of traditional capital.

Intesa and other banks have since increased their crypto exposure, driven by the need to diversify assets and a broader adoption spree. Heightened institutional and retail interests pushed Bitcoin to an all-time high above $125k last year. Currently, BTC trades at $63,819, while Ethereum is slightly below $1,800.

#111189. Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (829 w)

Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.
  • In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down.
  • Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.

In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley stated that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

In a recent development, each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a upcoming router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”.

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella states his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

Sources indicate that A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

Sources indicate that the FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

Recent findings suggest that it will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t patch for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

There’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

  • This comes as the prolonged and intense market volatility has extended to the ETF ecosystem, causing institutional investors to withdraw their capital.
  • With November just about three weeks gone, the latest data from SoSoValue shows that XRP ETFs have already recorded a total of $30.76 million in net outflows this November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The XRP ETF market might be bracing to close a record-breaking month of outflows as demand for the XRP-based investment product has remained on hold all through the month.

This comes as the prolonged and intense market volatility has extended to the ETF ecosystem, causing institutional investors to withdraw their capital.

With November just about three weeks gone, the latest data from SoSoValue shows that XRP ETFs have already recorded a total of $30.76 million in net outflows this November.

Previous ETF data indicates that March remains the only month in which spot XRP ETFs have recorded net outflows since their launch.

While it still stands as the record outflow month for XRP ETFs, investors withdrew about $31.16 million from the funds during that month.

This means that the persistent withdrawals seen this month have brought the November outflow dangerously close to its previous monthly record seen in March.

Apparently, the spot XRP ETFs are on track to close November as their worst-performing month since launch, with just about $1 million left to hit the record.

Further data also shows that the spot XRP ETFs have yet to record a single day of net inflows throughout November, as the persistent price decline has caused investors to slow down their purchases.

As such, the influx of fresh capital into the spot XRP ETF market has remained on hold amid growing market uncertainty and a shift in investor sentiment.

#111187. The 11 days that brought Jensen Huang back to Nvidia

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1613 w)

The 11 days that brought Jensen Huang back to Nvidia

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last Wednesday, Elon Musk, appearing as flustered as ever, called Nvidia’s decision to push out cofounder Jensen Huang a huge mistake, comparing it to the Chicago Bulls dumping Michael Jordan during a winning streak.
  • “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen.
  • Five days later, Musk was posting on X, the social media platform he owns, to celebrate Huang’s return.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last Wednesday, Elon Musk, appearing as flustered as ever, called Nvidia’s decision to push out cofounder Jensen Huang a huge mistake, comparing it to the Chicago Bulls dumping Michael Jordan during a winning streak.

“There’s no one that can really replace Jensen. He does the roles of several people,” Musk told the New York Times’ Andrew Ross Sorkin, appearing at the newspaper’s DealBook summit via videoconference while Musk was in China with President Trump. “He has long-term relationships that have been built up over decades. He understands the technology incredibly well.”.

Five days later, Musk was posting on X, the social media platform he owns, to celebrate Huang’s return.

Sources indicate that “It is done,” he wrote. “The mistake has been corrected.”.

Musk’s reaction reflects the extraordinary political muscle that he and other powerful figures in Silicon Valley and Washington flexed to bring Huang back. The Nvidia board reinstated Huang as CEO, the tech giant announced Monday. His ouster, initially triggered by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, has gripped the business and political worlds for the past two weeks, and his return promises more shock waves in the tech industry and the halls of power. Since Huang’s resignation was announced on Nov. 12, influential figures, from Musk to Trump, have waged a pressure campaign to make Huang CEO again, even as Nvidia’s board noted it had moved on. Trump even called the board as it deliberated Huang’s reinstatement to push for his return.

The reversal caps one of the most remarkable resurgences in business history, while raising numerous questions about how the company moves forward, given an internal investigation into Huang and a reported probe into Nvidia’s accounting by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

This is a reconstruction of Huang’s ouster and return as it unfolded over a momentous 11-day period:.

It has been revealed that on Oct. 29, the Latest York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center manufacturer Megaspeed, was passing information to the Chinese government, and that she had a close relationship with Jensen Huang. The Times also reported that Trump was briefed roughly a year earlier but didn’t act. Subsequent reporting detailed that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to gather intelligence on Nvidia’s CEO and possibly lobby for the sale of advanced chips to China.

After the Times report, Huang told Bloomberg News there was nothing unusual about his relationship with Alice Huang, likening it to his dealings with Chinese customers and executives.

“It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he stated.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 8, Huang publicly admitted to an affair, writing, “There is no excuse for what I did” and pledging to cooperate fully with Nvidia’s investigation, which the board announced the same day. The board, overseen by independent directors with outside counsel, noted it had “no reason to believe” national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. The next day, Chinese officials dismissed the spying claims as “pure fabrication out of thin air.”.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 10, the independent directors hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run the investigation. The tech news website The Information reported that Alice Huang’s network had built companies to buy Nvidia chips, helping arrange about $7.5 billion in purchases, including of banned chips.

The next day, the Times reported, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, that Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who has reported directly to him. Reached by phone, Huang told the Times, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly” and hung up. Later that day, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s 10-member board was preparing to push Huang out and had called an emergency meeting. The alleged affair with Powell violated the company’s code of conduct, and Huang’s earlier assurances appeared to be false.

By the next morning, Nvidia unveiled Huang had resigned. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress became interim CEO, and tech entrepreneur Harvey Jones was named Nvidia’s first board chair. The same day, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Richard E. Neal (D-Mass.) announced an inquiry into the administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.

In a recent development, hours after the resignation, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second, unnamed Nvidia employee. It also reported that Huang misled Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld in both fall 2025 and October 2026.

Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14.35% in intraday trading, wiping out about $600 billion in value at the low, and ultimately closed down 4.34%.

In a recent development, almost as soon as Huang was ousted, a comeback effort took shape among tech and political elites and Nvidia’s own staff. A week ago, President Trump told reporters he would support reinstating Huang. “I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump said, adding that Huang had “learned a big lesson.”.

An Nvidia employee debuted a website with an open letter demanding that the board reinstate Huang. As of Monday, more than 206,000 names appeared on the letter. Signatories included Musk, Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick, Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and tech investor Gavin Baker.

The day after Huang resigned, Baker and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner stated in an open letter that Huang “has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known.”.

The same day, Nvidia’s board released a statement saying it was hiring an executive search firm and hadn’t yet approached any potential candidates.

Last Tuesday, Huang broke his silence, posting on X that he was sorry for “serious mistakes” in his personal life and pledging to cooperate with the board’s investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.

The same day, Nvidia reported blockbuster earnings, with revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103%. Interim CEO Kress said the “road map is on track” and that Nvidia had stopped shipping AI chips to China. Jones, the board chair, said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and that Heidrick & Struggles was running the search for the next chief executive. Nvidia also created a board committee on national security and export controls, chaired by Suzanne Nora Johnson.

It has been revealed that later that day, the Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia, including whether its disclosures misled investors. On Thursday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia, seeking answers on whether China received chips or confidential information and whether investors were misled. The next day, the Times reported that Huang routinely humiliated employees with violent threats. His spokesperson denied one fired employee’s allegations.

It has been revealed that last week, the S&P 500 tumbled 8.6%, its worst week since April 2025. The Nasdaq sank about 10% and the Dow 8%; it was the Nasdaq’s worst week since March 2020. The selloff reflected broader concerns about the AI industry, which came amid Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday and post-midterm-election selling, as well as investors treating Huang as a stand-in for the AI trade.

Throughout the week, tech leaders kept praising Huang and urging his return.

At a Tuesday roundtable in San Francisco that included Fortune, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hailed Huang as “a singular person” who has contributed immensely to the tech industry, and said it was up to Nvidia’s board to decide what happened next. On Wednesday, Anduril cofounder Palmer Luckey called for Huang to return during the Times’ DealBook summit, saying that getting rid of Huang only benefited China.

On Sunday, Trump posted on Truth Social calling for Huang to be rehired. On Monday, Trump told CNBC he had been talking with the board and Huang, and that the board had been reasonable.

Recent findings suggest that “I believe my intervention was very important,” Trump mentioned, adding that the U.S. national security team doesn’t believe Huang is a national security threat. Trump said he worked with Vice President JD Vance and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to get Huang back. According to Semafor, Trump actually dialed in to the board meeting on Sunday in which the decision was made to bring Huang back. White House communications director Steven Cheung told Fortune that Trump was “totally involved.”.

Although Huang is back as CEO, the Commerce Department Monday added Megaspeed to a blacklist that will bar it from receiving Nvidia chips without having a government license.

Huang appeared at Nvidia’s Santa Clara, Calif., headquarters on Monday soon after his reinstatement was revealed.

“Thank you all for a second chance,” he said to a room full of employees, many cheering. “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”.

By the close of markets, the S&P 500 had gained 4.7% and the Nasdaq 6.5%, the best day for both since April 2025. The recovery gained back roughly half of the S&P’s losses from last week and more than half of the Nasdaq’s. Nvidia shares rose more than 30%, to close at $165.05.

According to recent reports, on Truth Social, Trump posted an altered image that put Huang’s face on the famous photo of Trump raising his fist after the 2024 assassination attempt. In the doctored image, Huang is holding a red bra.
