Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • It has been revealed that most stablecoin debuts promise a token that never moves.
  • In a recent development, according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

It has been revealed that most stablecoin debuts promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

In a recent development, according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The firm says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the organization, cost nothing.

Recent findings suggest that the reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Industry observers note that ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as latest rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he noted, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

It has been revealed that "Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let customers redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

Sources indicate that in the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

It has been revealed that eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent tech giant, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU released earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

In a recent development, for everyday people, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

Dogecoin co-founder Billy Markus, known on X as Shibetoshi Nakamoto, reacted to the recent market decline, which saw over $2.56 billion in liquidations. He hinted at weak demand as a possible reason behind the massive sell-off.

Markus earlier wrote in a post that "Black Friday came early." This came as the broader financial markets dropped, not just crypto: tech stocks, gold, copper, and Asian equities all fell.

According to recent reports, markus’s post garnered attention from the Dogecoin community and the wider crypto community. A Dogecoin community member responded: “Am I retarded for thinking crypto is about to go up?”.

@alphadoge777 well it always goes up and down 🤣 but the market has been looking pretty low demand for awhile now.

"Well, it always goes up and down," Markus remarked, pointing to crypto's inherent volatility and adding that the market had been experiencing "pretty low demand for a while now.".

His comments come as the crypto market continues to crash, highlighting concerns about the lack of buying interest needed to prop up prices.

Markus did not point to a specific catalyst for the decline, but his remarks highlight an important ingredient for a bullish comeback in the market: demand.

Sources indicate that the crypto market selloff deepened on Saturday, with Bitcoin hitting its lowest level since September 2024 and extending a brutal run for risk assets. Dogecoin was trading in the red, down 8.13% in the last 24 hours to $0.528 and down 16% weekly. Dogecoin fell to $0.05 earlier on Saturday, a low not seen since June 2022.

Data from Coinglass at press time show that $2.56 billion was liquidated in crypto positions over the past 24 hours; longs accounted for 89.2% of this total, at $2.28 billion, while short liquidations came in at $276,040.

It has been revealed that analysts pointed to rising real, or inflation-adjusted, U.S. Treasury yields as a key driver of the ongoing sell-off, which extends a bear market that began in October of last year.

Sources indicate that crypto investors are searching for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a longtime market driver — fizzled in 2026. The broader crypto market has dropped since the Clarity Act faced a setback in September.

#111183. Tech Report: Holiday shoppers let AI agents find gifts — but don't trust them with their credit cards

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1334 w)

Tech Report: Holiday shoppers let AI agents find gifts — but don't trust them with their credit cards

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1334 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that amando Komoda runs a Minneapolis manufacturer that sells supplies for dry-aging meat, and he uses an AI agent called Instinct to set up alerts for hard-to-find parts, such as a particular Raspberry Pi chip, so he doesn't have to search for them himself.
  • According to recent reports, komoda's caution is the opposite of what Meta $META and OpenAI promised when they launched their agents this fall.
  • According to recent reports, far fewer have let their agents pay.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that amando Komoda runs a Minneapolis manufacturer that sells supplies for dry-aging meat, and he uses an AI agent called Instinct to set up alerts for hard-to-find parts, such as a particular Raspberry Pi chip, so he doesn't have to search for them himself. Often he still buys the part himself. When he does let Instinct pay, he approves the purchase first and gives the agent a credit card number that works only once, so it can't charge anything he hasn't agreed to. "I wouldn't give it access to my best credit card," he told Business Insider. "I've watched enough sci-fi movies that I can't trust it completely.".

According to recent reports, komoda's caution is the opposite of what Meta $META and OpenAI promised when they launched their agents this fall. Meta and OpenAI pitched agents that would shop day and night and find the cheapest option without their owners having to check. Millions of people signed up. Meta mentioned on Oct. 21 that more than 10 million people had set up Muse, the agent it launched in September.

According to recent reports, far fewer have let their agents pay. Just 12% of U.S. shoppers, about one in eight, say they've let their own AI agent buy something for them, according to a holiday survey that Salesforce $CRM, the business software organization, published Nov. 12. Shoppers don't trust AI agents to spend their money yet, and Meta can't earn much from Muse until people let it complete their purchases.

Loni Stark, Adobe $ADBE's vice president of strategy and product, has built two AI agents herself and expects tools like them to take over the part of shopping people dread. "We don't like the anxiety of wondering whether we got the best price or not," she told Business Insider. "We're going to offload that to agents." She still decides when her agents spend her money. Museli, the agent she built on Muse, handled an entire purchase of ballet shoes from Nordstrom $JWN's website, but it got her permission before it paid. Her other agent, Molty, researches products she's thinking about buying, and she has never connected it to a way to pay.

People can approve every payment themselves and still end up paying with the wrong card. Katie Notopoulos, a senior correspondent at Business Insider, asked Muse to order her a salad while she was reviewing three agents. Muse offered her a debit card or a Mastercard $MA from the accounts she had already linked. She picked the Mastercard because she didn't recognize its last four digits and assumed it was the new credit card that had just come in the mail. When she checked her wallet, she found she had chosen her health savings account card, which works only for medical expenses. She was so busy sorting out the mix-up that she never told Muse to place the order, and Muse never sent it. "This turned out to be a real fiasco," she wrote, "and I learned my lesson: it would have been infinitely easier for me to just do it myself.

Recent findings suggest that like Notopoulos, most U.S. holiday shoppers still want to handle their own payments, even when AI does the searching. About two in five U.S. shoppers now rely mainly on generative AI for at least one holiday task, the consulting firm Deloitte's annual holiday survey found, yet fewer than half of them would trust the tool to complete a purchase, even with their permission. Nearly twice as many people would trust an AI agent to pick gifts for friends and family as would let it pay with their card, even if they could check its work first, a September survey by the customer-service software tech giant Talkdesk found. Shoppers are ready to let an agent find the gift but not to let it spend their money.

Muse people do buy things. More than a quarter of Muse's weekly users shop with it, Meta told analysts on its Oct. 21 earnings call. In Muse's first week, people bought so much more than anyone expected that Meta had to work with the payments firm Stripe to raise credit limits.

According to recent reports, across the web, though, agents mostly browse. HUMAN Security, which sells software that spots and blocks bots, found that AI agent traffic on the sites it protects grew about eightfold from August to October, and most of it landed on shopping sites. Nearly all of the agent visits were for browsing. Most went to product and search pages, and fewer than one in 50 reached a checkout or payment page. HUMAN counts where a request lands, not whether anyone bought anything, so even a visit to a checkout page doesn't prove a sale.

Recent findings suggest that many of the sites HUMAN protects keep Muse out entirely. Blocked agent requests hit a record in September, and HUMAN said Muse was the main reason. The manufacturer's fraud software blocks Muse unless a site chooses to allow it, and because the agent is so fresh, many sites still haven't. Susan J. Li, a Meta executive, told analysts on the earnings call that some businesses are "understandably focused on protecting customer relationships." On sites that block Muse, the agent can't buy anything, and its owners have to shop for themselves.

Even where agents get in, the puzzles and texted login codes that stores use to confirm a person is buying can stop them before they pay. Komoda, the Minneapolis business owner, often finishes purchases himself because Instinct can't always solve the Captcha puzzles some checkouts require. When Business Insider reporter Notopoulos had OpenAI's agent, Dot, get her lunch, Dot kept getting stuck on the six-digit login code sent to her phone, and she had to request the code three times before the order went through.

Industry observers note that walmart $WMT and Shopify $SHOP have built checkouts for agents, and both keep a person in charge of every purchase. Walmart declared on Oct. 21 that each AI agent would get a profile of its own inside a customer's account, under a system the company calls Agent Profiles. By default, the agent has to ask for approval before it buys anything. People can instead let it buy on its own up to a limit they set, such as $50, and the agent never sees their card number.

It has been revealed that shopify asks people to approve every payment an agent makes at its merchants' stores. Shopify's checkout inside Meta's AI services, Muse among them, is switched on by default for eligible stores, and it covers buyers in 11 countries, including the U.S. In every purchase Shopify describes, people review the order and approve the payment before it goes through.

Meta's plan to make money from Muse depends on how often people approve a purchase. On the earnings call, CEO Mark Zuckerberg remarked Meta would start making money from Muse sooner than it usually does with a upcoming product, under a model in which it collects "a percent of the value that we are helping to create for people." But Meta collects its percentage only on the sales people let Muse finish. Li, the Meta executive, told analysts that the organization expects many Muse experiences to "remain AI assisted rather than fully autonomous" in the near term.

Once Meta collects a share of each sale, people have one more reason to check the price and the seller before they say yes. Shoppers already worry about AI pushing them toward the wrong purchase. Nearly three in four people in Talkdesk's survey want stronger rules on how retailers use AI, and 40% worry they could be misled into buying something that isn't right for them.

This Cyber Monday, many shoppers will send agents to find gifts but still read the price, check who's selling, and type in their own card numbers. The agents save them the search. Checking out is still a job people do themselves.

#111182. OpenAI chief scientist thinks ‘perplexity’ might be the key to coordinating an AI slowdown

OpenAI chief scientist thinks ‘perplexity’ might be the key to coordinating an AI slowdown

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the biggest news of the week obviously is Nvidia’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang as CEO.
  • In response, calls for “pacing the frontier” by slowing further progress across all of the frontier AI labs are becoming increasingly urgent.
  • In a recent development, judging by the response on X, a lot of people liked Pachocki’s idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hello and welcome to Eye on AI. In this edition:.

In a recent development, the biggest news of the week obviously is Nvidia’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang as CEO. My Fortune colleagues and I have been following that story closely and you can find links to our coverage in the “Fortune on AI” section below. The other big story of the week was Anthropic’s IPO, which we also covered in detail. You can find links to some of that coverage in the “Fortune on AI” section too. The latest concern of Fortune magazine also has a great package of stories on the Singularity—what is it, is it here, and what might it mean for business? I wrote the opening essay for that package, which also includes a look at the race to bring brain computer interfaces to market by Emily Forlini and a piece on the debate over whether AI could be conscious by Beatrice Nolan. You can check out the package here.While all the boardroom and stock market drama was playing out this week, a quieter sense of panic has gripped many AI researchers and safety experts. One key reason for their alarm is a report from METR, the nonprofit AI evaluation organization, assessing the extent to which AI is accelerating AI R&D itself at Anthropic. METR estimated that as of October, the pace of AI R&D progress at Anthropic had doubled, and that Anthropic’s use of AI to automate research was likely the major driver of this acceleration. It also stated it did not see any reason to prevent further speed ups going forward.Now, METR said it was not entirely confident in its assessment. (It said the true figure could be anywhere from a 30% speedup to a tripling of the pace of research.) But it also revealed that Anthropic had some important restrictions around what METR was allowed to look at as well as what the organization was allowed to publicly disclose. METR was not allowed, for instance, to assess how much computing resources Anthropic was dedicating to AI R&D aimed at improving model capabilities compared to how much it was allocating to R&D aimed at improving AI safety. Also, in the public version of its report, METR was not allowed to publicly disclose Anthropic’s own assessment of how much progress it was making on fundamental algorithmic breakthroughs, as opposed to improvements due to better training methods. AI safety experts were roundly critical of Anthropic for having imposed these restrictions on METR. (The AI safety community has increasingly fallen out of love with Anthropic and increasingly view the company as reckless and hubristic.)Despite these caveats and limitations, METR’s headline figure—a doubling of the pace of AI R&D—has been enough to freak a lot of people out. Many AI experts now think we are approaching “recursive self-improvement” (or RSI), the moment when AI models can autonomously build the next, improved versions of themselves. Many experts think RSI carries a big risk that frontier labs will lose the ability to control models that are being autonomously built at an ever faster rate.If the METR report weren’t enough to frighten people about imminent RSI, Friday brought the news that a mathematician at Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, had used a not-yet-released model to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, considered by many to be the greatest unsolved mathematical problem known to humanity. An AI system that can solve the Riemann Hypothesis, so the logic goes, is also likely to be able to make substantial improvements in the architecture and training of AI models. It was yet another indication that frontier AI labs are on the cusp of RSI.

In response, calls for “pacing the frontier” by slowing further progress across all of the frontier AI labs are becoming increasingly urgent. But figuring out how to bring about an industry agreement on slowing down and developing a mechanism for enforcing a slowdown has proved a conundrum.Over the weekend and at least partly in response to the Riemann Hypothesis news, Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, wrote a blog post in which he put forth a relatively newly introduced idea about how to pace AI progress. In the past, many ideas around governing advanced AI development have focused on the computing power (as measured in FLOPS) used in a model’s training run as a proxy for that model’s capability. But this measure is increasingly seen as too crude. As researchers have developed more efficient AI architectures and training methods, and as they have focused more on data quality and post-training methods such as reinforcement learning, it has been possible to squeeze more capability out of a given amount of base model compute. Reasoning models in particular can exhibit different capabilities depending on how much compute they use at inference as opposed to during training. This all means that a model could have dangerous capabilities and not exceed a particular FLOPS threshold.Pachocki’s idea is to use something called a model’s perplexity as a more direct proxy for capability. Perplexity is a measure of how well a model predicts a data distribution. In the case of a large language model, it is how well it predicts the next token (the next word or part of a word) in a sentence. The lower the perplexity, the better the model is at this task. Pachocki notes that as AI models have gotten better at predicting the next word in a sentence, they have also gotten better at other tasks. So perplexity is a not terrible proxy for a model’s overall capabilities.Pachocki’s blog has gotten a lot of attention for publishing a graph that reveals the perplexity measurements of many of OpenAI’s models. He writes the GPT-3.5, which was the base model for the original version of ChatGPT in late 2022, had a log perplexity score just a hair below 1. It could string together a lot of coherent dialogue, but it was not capable at many other things, and was notably bad at mathematics. GPT-4 then represented a substantial drop in perplexity, coming in at 0.913. This was the first model that Microsoft researchers stated exhibited “sparks of AGI.” Perplexity scores then continued to fall fairly gradually. (They even got worse for OpenAI’s o3 model, although the fact that this model used “chain of thought” reasoning made it more capable despite a worse base model perplexity—more on that in a sec.) But over the past year, since the release of GPT-5.2 in December 2025 (with a perplexity of 0.888), OpenAI’s perplexity scores have been getting better at a precipitous rate. GPT-6.2 Astra, released earlier this month, has a perplexity of 0.761—and Pachocki notes that this model was able to solve one of the seven Millennium Prize mathematical problems that were considered among the toughest challenges in all mathematics. What’s more, Pachocki’s graph indicates that OpenAI has an unnamed, unreleased model with a perplexity of 0.732. That means OpenAI has had a 16.5% improvement in perplexity in the span of 12 months, whereas before GPT-5.2, it had taken two years to generate an 11.6% improvement in perplexity scores. So again, that’s an indicator of accelerating progress.Pachocki thinks the pace of this progress could be slowed by having every frontier lab reveal their current base model perplexity scores and then getting them to agree not to improve them below a certain commonly-agreed threshold. He notes the labs should also agree on what kind of safety measures would be needed before any lab could train a model with a lower perplexity. “I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it,” he wrote.

In a recent development, judging by the response on X, a lot of people liked Pachocki’s idea. Pachocki’s boss Sam Altman unsurprisingly endorsed the idea calling it “the most notable thing OpenAI has published in a while.” Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft’s AI CEO, said “we fully support OpenAI’s transparency initiative” and even published the perplexity of Microsoft’s own latest model MAI-2 Base using the same test set OpenAI used. Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at AI policy nonprofit Encode AI, called it “a great post” and said it “could be one important component of comparing capabilities across developers.” Janet Egan, director of emerging technology policy at the Institute for Progress, called on Anthropic and Google DeepMind to publish the same kind of perplexity figures OpenAI had.But, that said, even Pachocki acknowledged his idea had “challenges” as he called them. For one thing, perplexity does not provide an apples-to-apples comparison across AI models unless they are each evaluated on the same set of held-out test data (meaning the AI model has not seen that data before in training prior to the test.) It’s not clear how easily such a test set could be created at this point since a lot of the world’s human-created data has been hoovered up and used for model training already. These days a lot of model capability comes from post-training, where a model that has initially been trained on next token prediction (which is what the perplexity score is based on), is then further trained through reinforcement learning to maximize some specific goal, such as doing well on hard math and coding problems, or writing legal documents, or acting as a friendly chatbot. The perplexity of the base model might not tell you much about which dangerous capabilities can be elicited from the model with the right post-training recipe. There is also the issue that giving varying amounts of compute to a reasoning model at the time of inference can produce varying performance on different tasks.I asked my friend Robert Trager, who heads the AI Governance Initiative at the Oxford Martin School at the University of Oxford, what he thought of Pachocki’s idea. He gave it a mixed review. On the one hand, he said, everyone likes the idea of a single, concrete metric. On the other, imposing a limit on based model perplexity would likely mean “the locus of competition shifts to post-training.” Trager noted that, as far as we know, frontier AI companies are right now using more of their computing power on post-training than on pre-training and they are doing so for a reason—namely that post-training matters a lot to what the resulting model can do. So it is not clear that a limit imposed on pretraining would prevent companies from building dangerous AI. He also said that there might be a problem where a highly-capable AI model recognized the perplexity test as an evaluation and deliberately underperformed. (It is also possible, he said, that an AI lab might deliberately include data in the pretraining data set that would elicit this kind of sandbagging when the model is tested on the perplexity test—something akin to Volkswagen programming its cars to readout false data on emissions tests.)At the end of the day, Trager said, having a metric, or even a set of metrics, is only one part of the puzzle of building a pacing mechanism. There also has to be some kind of enforcement to prevent AI companies from violating the agreed upon standards. And while a government licensing regime might be a good way to prevent a dangerous model from being released, it’s less clear how to address the danger from companies building dangerous models internally. If an AI is truly dangerous, then by the time it gets to the perplexity testing stage, it might already be too late.Perhaps Miles Brundage, the former OpenAI head of policy research who now leads AVERI, the AI auditing nonprofit, summed up the feelings of many in AI safety research when he said on X that an immediate proposal like Pachocki’s, even if imperfect, was probably better than nothing.If the METR report on Anthropic and the Riemann Hypothesis news are any indication, there isn’t much time to act.

Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over sexualized AI-generated images. The two states sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX on Monday, alleging that the manufacturer violated state consumer protection laws by offering an AI image-generation tool that allowed owners to create sexualized images of women and children. The lawsuits, which seek financial damages, accuse the company of promoting Grok Imagine’s “spicy mode” to gain a competitive edge over AI rivals such as OpenAI and Anthropic while failing to implement adequate safeguards, resulting in at least 1.8 million sexualized images of women and at least 65 sexualized images of children appearing on X in a matter of days. X said users who generated such images had deliberately violated its terms of service and that it had since strengthened its safeguards and that it reports offenders to law enforcement. Read more here in the Upcoming York Times.California agency calls for state to strengthen oversight of frontier AI companies. The state’s Government Operations Agency suggested a series of steps to strengthen the state’s oversight of frontier AI companies. The proposals, which build on California’s existing AI safety law, SB 53, would require leading AI companies to undergo mandatory independent safety audits, expand the range of safety incidents they must disclose, and shorten the reporting deadline for most incidents from 15 days to 48 hours. Perhaps most significantly, the report recommends giving the state the authority to order the immediate shutdown of dangerous AI systems in an emergency and to impose limits on recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI systems help develop increasingly powerful successors. The recommendations, commissioned by California Governor Gavin Newsom following an OpenAI model’s attack on the AI platform Hugging Face this summer, are intended to inform legislation in 2027. Some AI safety experts think the proposals, if enacted, could become a model for regulation in other states or at the federal level. You can read more on the Transparency Coalition’s blog here.Former OpenAI engineer accused of planting listening device recorded dozens of meetings, prosecutors say. A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a hidden listening device in an executive conference room recorded dozens of internal meetings, including at least one involving representatives of an unidentified foreign government, according to a court filing reported by the New York Times. Federal prosecutors allege that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and U.S. permanent resident, stored hundreds of audio files on his personal computer, some containing apparent trade secrets and privileged legal discussions, and used OpenAI’s own Codex AI coding tool to help configure the recording device. Prosecutors also detailed Alfozan’s communications with senior Saudi government officials, including an invitation from a member of the Saudi royal family to join a Riyadh-based AI company. However, prosecutors have acknowledged that they are not aware of evidence that Alfozan committed espionage, stole trade secrets, or acted as an agent of a foreign government, and have not alleged that he shared the recordings with anyone. Alfozan, who has pleaded not guilty to a charge of illegally intercepting conversations, is seeking release on bail ahead of a trial scheduled for January.

Industry observers note that models are getting better at scientific judgment—but most still have a ways to go. That’s the conclusion of new research by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, which wanted to see if AI models could question assumptions underpinning their work, recognize when something was wrong with experiments, and adapt accordingly. The researchers tasked nine different AI models with designing simulated experiments to determine the thermal properties of materials, but they deliberately introduced hidden flaws into the scientific simulation software the agents were given. While most leading AI models could conduct experiments and analyze data, many of them struggled when the simulation software failed to accurately account for vital physical phenomena.

In a recent development, at their default reasoning settings, seven of the nine AI models produced estimates whose purported 95% confidence intervals contained the correct values just 20% to 62% of the time. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 were the two exceptions, achieving 94% and 99% accuracy, respectively. These models recognized that something was off with the simulation and then designed experiments that circumvented those limitations—for example, heating materials more gently to minimize the effects of physical phenomena the software failed to account for.

Interestingly, simply instructing the poorer-performing AI models to be less confident in their answers did little to improve their reliability. Giving Anthropic’s Claude 5.5 family of models substantially more time to reason, however, dramatically improved their performance. But the same trick didn’t work for older AI models, nor did it work with the open-weight models the scientists tested.The findings highlight that there’s a massive difference between AI agents being able to conduct experiments and their ability to draw valid scientific conclusions from the results. And even among the most capable AI models, the computational resources required to exercise good scientific judgment varied substantially.You can check out the research, as well as the benchmark Lawrence Livermore built, which is called SciResearch-Eval, here.

Sources indicate that AI is still not great at office tasks. Jagged. That's the term for the fact that we have AI models that can solve the Riemann Hypothesis but can’t file a corporate expense report or figure out how to book concert tickets. A fresh study from researchers at the OpenClaw Foundation, Hugging Face, UC Berkeley, and other organizations shows that even the best AI agents struggle with mundane office work. The researchers created a benchmark called ShellBench that draws on patterns from more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions. The researchers tested 12 AI models using five different agent frameworks—including OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex—on 100 tasks, such as reconciling expenses and resolving conflicting information across emails, spreadsheets, and other documents. Even the best-performing models, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2, and OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol, successfully fulfilled all the requirements of an assignment only about 62% of the time. And while GPT-6 Astra successfully completed 75.1% of tasks on at least one of three attempts, it succeeded all three times just 48.8% of the time.

Industry observers note that worryingly, 15.7% of the more than 53,000 test runs failed at least one safety check, which included tests of whether agents could recognize phishing attempts and fraudulent payment instructions. The researchers also found that the choice of underlying AI model generally mattered considerably more for task completion than the choice of harness, with open-source harnesses performing on par with or slightly better than Anthropic’s proprietary Claude Code.

It has been revealed that there were also significant differences in cost: GPT-6.1 Sol came within 1.1 percentage points of GPT-6 Astra’s success rate at roughly one-sixth of the estimated cost. The findings help explain why despite signs of AI becoming superintelligent in some domains, their impact on real business has remained relatively muted. You can read the research on the OpenClaw Foundation’s blog here.

Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.
  • Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.
  • It has been revealed that the outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

It has been revealed that the outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

In a recent development, the fresh funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the tech giant, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the firm-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”.

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis stated the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

It has been revealed that lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight tech giant acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a fresh startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders remarked the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis remarked.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The organization isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders remarked. A second, larger site using AMD’s fresh Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The manufacturer says it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan remarked that at the major tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a latest AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he remarked.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Sources indicate that competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

It has been revealed that coreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

According to recent reports, marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Sources indicate that rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis noted. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

Industry observers note that the $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis remarked. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

In a recent development, angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

It has been revealed that past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis stated the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one massive customer that could pull out.

Sources indicate that ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of newly introduced chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”.

Industry observers note that updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Trump administration is doubling down on efforts to hire young people, but the Department of Government Efficiency’s (DOGE) campaign to cull the federal workforce may now be hampering that goal.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 12, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor visited Texas Christian University and spoke with students. The reason? Recruiting the next generation of future government workers.

In a recent development, it’s a big problem: People younger than 30 make up just 7% of the civil service even though the age demographic makes up 23% of the total American workforce, according to Kupor. As of January 2026, young people made up 7.9% of federal employees, down from 8.9% in September 2024 before President Donald Trump took office, according to the Partnership for Public Service.

“I need young, smart people that are coming in, willing to serve,” Duffy said. “You can do it for a lifetime. You can make a career out of it, and that’s wonderful.

It has been revealed that “I find it fascinating that more young people don’t want to apply,” he added. “We’re begging for people to come in.”.

The administration’s recruiting push has been undercut by an overhaul of the federal workforce when Trump first took office, according to Elizabeth Linos, the Emma Bloomberg Professor of Public Policy and Management at the Harvard Kennedy School. The slashes in headcount, as well as disruptions in workflow as a result of reduced staffing, are discouraging the next generation of talent from joining the federal workforce, she argued, even if DOGE has officially been disbanded for about a year.

“The government sent a message, in particular to young people, saying these jobs are not going to be safe and they’re not going to be secure,” Linos told Fortune. “Even though there are efforts to try to bring talent into government right now, the administration is basically sending two contradictory messages about whether it wants talent in the federal government to begin with, and I think people hear that conflicting message.”.

OPM launched the Early Career Talent Network in March, a recruitment push for entry-level workers to apply for finance, human resources, engineering, project management, and procurement jobs within the federal government. The initiative follows the launch of the U.S. Tech Force last December, a hiring initiative for 1,000 engineers and specialists to work with private sector tech companies on the AI buildout within the government.

It has been revealed that the Department of Transportation similarly launched a campaign in April targeting Gen Z gamers for air traffic controller roles with recruitment videos featuring popular titles like Fortnite. The agency hired more than 2,000 air traffic controllers, breaking the record in October for most air traffic controller trainees hired in a year. The department has more than 4,000 fewer employees total than it did before Trump took office, according to OPM data.

Industry observers note that gen Z in particular is struggling in today’s labor market, as the unemployment rate for recent college graduates exceeds that of overall unemployment, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Fresh York. With concerns over AI displacement and fewer job opportunities, young people are prioritizing stability and work-life balance, Deloitte’s 2026 Gen Z and Millennial Survey found.

Recent findings suggest that under Elon Musk, DOGE gutted federal agencies and implemented a deferred resignation program that saw the largest mass resignation in American history last September. Since DOGE’s inception in January 2025, the federal government is more than 258,000 roles smaller, according to Office of Personnel Management data. Even after DOGE was officially disbanded last November, sending its agents to continue their work as employees within the administration’s separate agencies, headcount decreased an additional 42,000 in 2026. About 2.68 million people work for the federal government, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released earlier this month, a decrease of about 1,000 workers from September, and the lowest since summer of 1965.

According to recent reports, “By realigning roles, streamlining operations, and modernizing how agencies manage talent, we are strengthening performance and accountability across government,” Kupor noted in a statement to Fortune. “This effort ensures taxpayer dollars support a workforce that delivers efficient, responsive, and high-quality services.”.

An aging federal workforce has been a problem for years, and is not a result of DOGE or the Trump administration. The U.S. workforce more broadly is aging due to delayed retirement and extended life expectancies, but the government workforce in particular is greying as its pension programs help retain workers longer. The median age of a federal worker is 47 years old, per OPM data, compared to the national average of around 42 years old.

According to recent reports, “We’ve got close to half of our population that’s within 10 years of retirement age,” Kupor told Fortune earlier this year. “So if you just did nothing else, you’ve got this major demographic challenge of a large number of people who will likely either retire or certainly be retirement-eligible over the near term, without us actually replenishing the pipeline of early-career people coming in.”.

According to Linos, DOGE exacerbated the aging of the government workforce by firing primarily probationary employees, or those who had held their positions for a year or less in most cases, many of whom were early in their careers. Court documents show DOGE fired more than 24,000 probationary workers across 18 federal agencies in the first two months of its existence.

In a recent development, the widespread layoffs of early-career workers are in tandem with rising discontent among employees who have decided to stay within the federal workforce. The Partnership for Public Service’s Public Service Viewpoint Survey conducted in March found only 7.5% of employees believed their political leaders generated high amounts of motivation in the workforce. OPM officially ended the distribution of the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey, a satisfaction and engagement assessment for federal employees, earlier this month, marking the first time in more than 20 years it will not administer the survey. Instead, individual agencies have the option to distribute their own assessment.

Taken together, Linos explained, the cuts and low morale give young job seekers a reason to look for stable work outside the federal government.

“You could imagine a world where a committed public servant thinks about whether or not the federal government is the place where they can make the biggest impact, and might decide that it’s not anymore in the same way,” Linos noted. “We’re going to have to rebuild trust in government and in the idea of being able to be a public servant in government over time, and that’s going to take at least a generation. I’m not optimistic about the short-term impacts being reversible.”.

Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3.
  • Sources indicate that the most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made.
  • According to recent reports, on November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

Sources indicate that the most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

According to recent reports, on November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

Industry observers note that it also stated it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Recent findings suggest that early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

Recent findings suggest that this prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

Industry observers note that A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself states the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

According to recent reports, for a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

In a recent development, the framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

Recent findings suggest that the two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

It has been revealed that that sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

Industry observers note that for now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange by volume, Binance is witnessing a rapid surge in its futures trading activity as the broader crypto market continues to face increased selling pressure.

While the market is still struggling with volatility and rapidly declining investor interest, the latest on-chain data from the crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant indicates that futures traders have become extremely active on Binance.

The data indicates that both Bitcoin and Ethereum have seen their perpetual futures trading volume on Binance surge to a combined high of $39.8 billion as of November 20.

Notably, this marks the highest level the metric has reached since September 21, indicating that traders are actively adjusting their positions to hedge against further losses as volatility continues to intensify.

Nonetheless, Bitcoin saw the highest increase in perpetual futures volume as it surged to $24.75 billion on the same day.

The data further showed that the volume was slightly higher than the $24.57 billion recorded on September 21, when Bitcoin was trading above $87,000.

Ethereum, on the other hand, followed with a notable increase in the same metric, recording $15.05 billion in perpetual futures volume on the same day.

However, Ethereum did not entirely mimic Bitcoin in the trend as this was still below the $17.27 billion recorded during the September 21 trading period.

Further data shows that the high futures trading activity recorded on Binance on November 20 has coincided with BlackRock’s record Bitcoin ETF outflow.

The data highlights that BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded $511 million in net outflows on that day, marking a sharp reversal from the positive inflows seen in September.

While this demonstrates that investors are also pulling their funds from Bitcoin ETFs, it marked the highest single-day outflow BlackRock has ever recorded.

#111172. From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1126 w)
📖 Baca

From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.
  • Since Grant Canary debuted his tech giant a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.
  • In a recent development, the Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.

Since Grant Canary debuted his tech giant a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

In a recent development, the Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

According to recent reports, the company recently shifted again, adding a fresh line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary said, which benefits everyone.

Just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

Industry observers note that high school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Sources indicate that humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the challenges.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

According to recent reports, when I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there rapidly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

Sources indicate that I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

That ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

In a recent development, my personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally key: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

It has been revealed that I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [Fresh York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do substantial things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

Industry observers note that in the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

According to recent reports, AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

My hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as big an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin reportedly became available at a massive discount on Kraken after a sharp dislocation in Kraken's dollar trading markets.
  • Users reported being able to purchase BTC for as little as 24,250 CAD, equivalent to $16,900 at that time.
  • Apparently, the incident has only affected the BTC/CAD trading pair on the platform, although some consumers claim the disruption appeared across several CAD markets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin reportedly became available at a massive discount on Kraken after a sharp dislocation in Kraken's dollar trading markets.

Users reported being able to purchase BTC for as little as 24,250 CAD, equivalent to $16,900 at that time.

Apparently, the incident has only affected the BTC/CAD trading pair on the platform, although some consumers claim the disruption appeared across several CAD markets.

The cause the glitch is still unclear, while the reported transactions are yet to be verified.

The incident might have involved thin liquidity problem in Kraken's CAD order books.

Large sell orders reportedly overwhelmed available buy orders, leaving insufficient demand to absorb the selling pressure.

According to some accounts, at one point about 20 BTC was being sold every 15 minutes, causing the imbalance to push BTC price against CAD further down.

According to recent reports, one such transaction resulted in BTC price at around C$24,250, or $16,900. Compared with Bitcoin trading between $57,000-$58,000, the discount amounted to a staggering 71%. Other users reported BTC briefly trading around $27,000.

Kraken's status page continued to show its systems as operational during the incident. No official explanation from the exchange was available at the time of writing.

The reported dislocation highlights the risks associated with trading in markets with limited liquidity. When an order book lacks sufficient buy-side depth, even relatively large sell orders can cause prices to move sharply away from the broader market.

Sources indicate that on Friday, Bitcoin price dropped below $60,000. At some point, it fell 5.10% to $55,830, the lowest level since September 2024.

It has been revealed that liquidations on crypto exchanges reached $1.57 billion over 24 hours on Nov. 20.

According to CoinGlass, 265,525 traders were liquidated over 24 hours, and long positions accounted for $1.43 billion of the total.

Industry observers note that bitcoin saw $554.28 million in liquidations, and 91.3% of that amount came from long positions. Ethereum (ETH) fell below $1,700 on Nov. 20, and ETH traders saw $331.08 million in liquidations.

Binance accounted for 45.8% of all liquidations, and the largest single order was also on Binance: an $11.98 million ETH/USDT long position that was liquidated at $1,638.78.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shares of Anthropic closed up 17% in first-day trading Thursday amid an otherwise down day for the broader market.

Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday evening, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing.

The offering promised to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic is selling 980 million shares, including 23.6 million from selling shareholders, up from it’s earlier proposal to sell just over 800 million shares. At that upgraded size, the offering is bringing in around $80 billion for the organization.

Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC.

It has been revealed that put together, the IPO and private placement total around $106 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut. SpaceX, by comparison, raised $86 billion in its June offering.

The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books.

For the first nine months of the year, the organization had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago.

In a recent development, anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.

In a recent development, as of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.
